"Life is short 

And art is long,

The occasion instant, Experiment perilous, 

Decision difficult."

PREFACE 

"The laws of a nation form the most instructive part of its history," writes Gibbon. In its laws and trials a people's true ideals appear. No age has had so many laws as ours, and 

Massachusetts is well to the front in the number of its enactments. Dr. Johnson would stamp this as a sign of degeneracy. "A corrupt society," he asserts, "has many laws." Our instructive history, however, belies Dr. Johnson. We have many laws because we seek by laws not to punish and to subdue, but to protect and to inspire. Our enactments establish our idealism, and our idealism, like our desire for progress, knows no bounds. Hatred of the offender in this Commonwealth is not so dynamic legislatively as solicitude for the injured. 

The history of Massachusetts supports Gibbon's epigram. A lawsuit against inhabitants of Ipswich, one of our earliest settlements, seems responsible for the first judicial utterance as to the status of our citizens. Chief Justice Joseph Dudley upholding a levy of taxes by the tyrannical Andros in that case, is said to have declared, "The laws of England will not follow the colonists to the far ends of the earth. The colonists do not differ from slaves except that they are not bought and sold." 

Here was a dictum often to be quoted for the overthrow of the principle which it sought to establish. It not only displays the opinion of a descendant of one of the earliest settlers, but illustrates the pompousness of the courts of that day, their willingness to offend, and, an unfortunate characteristic still found in many of our most conscientious altruists, lack of understanding of the sensitiveness, self-respect, and earnest endeavor of our everyday citizens, and of their willingness to fight to protect possible infringements on their remotely endangered liberties. Perhaps the dictum tended to unify revolutionary tendencies; it created among greater numbers, and aroused throughout the colony, a serious and judicious conviction that judicial decisions, if they offend the majority, must not stand. The words did much to cause the "Glorious Revolution of 1689." As a definition of status, they set the low watermark of our political history.

vi 

PREFACE 

From the days of Chief Justice Dudley the people have steadily progressed in their power directly to control all bodies of the government except the courts. A long line of competent justices, in the lower courts as well as in the Supreme Judicial Court, has satisfied the people that our judicial system, though not perfect, is sound. The citizens turn to the legislature for their redress, and with the referendum and initiative as added checks and balances, have faith. 

Our many laws have been enacted because our people have determined to procure in the fullest sense, liberty and enlightenment. They seek to attain and to hold these with governmental assistance and assurances, and to secure for themselves and posterity not only justice but advancement, without being obliged to purchase them. Though our earliest "Blue Laws,” based on the desire to create a Biblical Commonwealth, sought, to a great extent, to control the morals of the colony, yet the greatest of the commandments, which summarized the law and the prophets, was the theme of those enactments. Those laws were created that divine worship might be uniform and universal. With less frequency the principles of the second great commandment, like unto the first, as defined by that heckling lawyer immortalized by the tenth chapter of St. Luke, were the basis of the early colonial laws; and legislation did not always carry the theme, "Thou shalt love thy neighbor as thyself."

Our more recent statutes seem for the protection of our neighbor. At first the legislature aimed to protect him chiefly in his rights of property; but the great, later tendency is to protect him in his everyday life from the carelessness, thoughtlessness, and wilfulness of his neighbor. He is protected not only in his property and person, but in his right and power to earn, in his health, in his peace of mind, in his opportunity to study, to learn, and by honest merit to advance. Since Joseph Dudley's day legislation on such subjects has become a recognized function of the Commonwealth. As a result of that legislation, a state, in but a little over two centuries, has arisen from a durance wherein the inhabitants by a decree of the highest court of the colony differed from slaves only in that they were not bought and sold, to a Commonwealth among the richest, most enlightened, and most progressive in the world; under such circumstances our legislature is not to be criticized if its enactments have been voluminous. 

These numerous enactments create almost chaos in the law. 

More than ever "Law is a bottomless pit," and perhaps, as

PREFACE 

vii Arbuthnot further remarks, "a cormorant, a cormorant, a Harpy that devours everything. Though Plautus in his sophism "little do you know what a gloriously uncertain thing the law is," expresses a warning worthy of consideration, yet the situation is not so hopeless as Arbuthnot would have us believe. To be sure, to search the authorities in strict compliance with the case system, to all but a lover of learning, is tedious, and even to those most in love with their great profession, is laborious; clearly if a practitioner in his daily work does this, he must appreciate the comment of Lord Eldon, "To live by the bar you must live like a hermit and work like a horse." Those who conscientiously and thoroughly examine the authorities, unify and set down the results, exchange for their finished manuscript, man's only mortal asset, a lifetime. The ordinary practitioner, if his best energies are set to protect the rights of his clients, of the courts, and of the state, cannot and will not attempt this. It is with the desire to assist such men and to aid in the clarifying of a complicated legal subject, that this book is written. 

Butcher and Lang in their introduction to their translation of Homer's Odyssey assert that any translation cannot outlast the era in which it is written. If this is true of a great modern classic, a translation of the most ancient and the greatest of all classics, a text on a subject as progressive as the law, must be short lived. In law a short life may be useful, and utility is our aim.

This work aims to assist a lawyer in the preparation of his case, and when a ready reference is requested in the course of trial, to furnish one. It aims at speed in preparation and in trial. The attempt is to index thoroughly, to summarize each subject at the beginning of each chapter, and to set forth not only the principles of law but usually a quotation from, or a summary of, the case which decides the point. The footnotes are not to be regarded as mere references; frequently these embody important matters which are simply suggested by the text. This is intentionally so. The text leads the reader quickly to the principle sought; the footnote usually sets forth that principle and gives the foundation for a brief. 

This work is submitted with the hope that it will tend to aid in establishing a true justice. I realize with Cicero that "Strict law is often a great injustice," and that one with knowledge of the law may impose on the weak and ignorant. This text may help to show what the law of evidence and of trial is; to

viii PREFACE 

lessen the instances where law shall cause injustice and to make knowledge of the law more accessible. It may enable those so inclined to place the errors in these subjects, that they may be corrected, and that the whole law of trials may be unified and reduced to code. 

Lawrence, Mass.

June 1, 1931

I. Introductory. "Justice is the end of government. It is the end of civil society. It ever has been, ever will be pursued until it be obtained or until liberty be lost in the pursuit." The pursuit of a just system of trial has continued through many centuries in many lands and among many races. It still continues. The trail frequently has been lost in one part of the world only again to be picked up in far distant provinces and by a different people. That honest, conscientious people in accordance with recognized legal institutions have taken the lives of their neighbors as a result of facts established by trial by battle, by water, or by fire, and that a suspected person could legally have been apprehended by, and must legally have been obliged to surrender himself into the hands of, a wild and infuriated mob on "hue and cry" shock the modern sense of justice. Yet these methods kept the king's peace and under them apparently a happy people lived and grew in numbers and wealth. In all civilized and semi-civilized groups,-in fact in all communities where men through generations have lived together, some method of punishing the perpetrator of recognized crimes and of protecting property has existed. Furthermore considerable uniformity seems embodied in the fundamental laws of mankind.¹

The study of evidence concerns not so much the fundamental laws as the methods of determining fact; and though the world has tried various methods none other so far has held the confidence of so many people for so long a time as the "jury system."

The jury system whether a creation of its various claimants, the near East, Rome, Germany or England,-has become so modified by modern legislation that its originators and many of its ardent supporters in former centuries, might doubt its present honesty and usefulness. Fundamentally a jury was a body of the people chosen by and from the people. No minor body of men who might be associated with political, commercial, financial or other interests passed on the efficiency or capability of prospective jurors. No lists were printed and published of persons who might be called to serve in the trials of the state or of individuals. A community apparently met and honored the opinion of its assembled men to the extent of considering that if twelve believed a man guilty of crime he should be 

1 See Spencer's "Synthetic Philosophy."

THE COURT 

7 sent to trial. For the trial, jurors were drawn from the assembled inhabitants of the county. They were sworn, tried the case and returned their verdict. If there was a representative of the king present he was rather to maintain order than to pass on questions of fact or admissibility of evidence. The less that he had to say the better the satisfaction. There were no complicated rules of evidence. The proceeding was brief and inspired confidence because it was the act of the people themselves. Few early attempts by statute to change methods of procedure were made, and the one attempt in early colonial days ended in a failure so astonishing that it led its most conscientious promoters to repentance and confession of error.2 

2 The following editorial from the 

Boston Herald on or about March 22, 1912, is worthy of note: "A Massachusetts instance. Popular clamor as a substitute for the sober and deliberate processes of justice has had one notable and melancholy exemplification in the history of Massachusetts. The story of that episode is one upon which New England is never glad to dwell, but it nevertheless points a moral in these times when it is seriously proposed to regard truth as a matter of majorities and to have a count of noses, wherever they are found, take the place of the opinions of the trained specialists in the law.

When the witchcraft delusion of 1692 

seized the province the people would not wait for the workings of the established tribunal of justice. It was too slow to suit them. No doubt they feared that it would be 'reactionary' or inclined to be too respectful to the letter of the law. So they cried out for a special court to hustle along the trial of the witches, and Gov. Phipps weakly yielded to the clamor and named seven judges to conduct the trials.

It was distinctly a popular court, and was controlled absolutely by the popular will. Not a single one of the seven judges was a lawyer. Two of the judges were clergymen, two were physicians, and three were merchants.

The common law was thrown aside, rules of evidence were ignored, and the judges and juries were left untrammelled by any 'quibbles of the law' to follow their own feelings and the popular will. 

Says Washburn in his 'Judicial His tory of Massachusetts': "The trials were but a form of executing popular vengeance. Juries were intimidated by the frowns and persuasions of the court, and by the outbreakings of the multitude that crowded the place of trial, to render verdicts, against their own consciences and judgment.' He cites one case, that of Rebecca Nurse, in which the jury actually had the courage to bring in a verdict of not guilty. 

Whereupon the accusers raised a great outery and the judges were overcome by the clamor.' The jury was sent back, returned with a verdict of guilty, and the woman was accordingly executed. Thus promptly and effectively did the popular will succeed in bringing about the judicial decision it wanted.

Witchcraft delusions are no more, but from time to time other delusions hardly less unreasonable and dangerous arise. One of the functions of our courts is to protect the people against themselves. The popular clamor which would upset the established judicial system and put the administration of justice into hasty and untrained hands is not always more safe and sane in the twentieth century than it was in the seventeenth."'

Witches, Winsor's and 

Washburn "History of Massachusetts." 

See also records of the Witch Trials at the Salem Court House.

In modern times the departure from the old system is great; and with the departure confidence in the system is somewhat shaken. In final analysis, however, the system stands because those with power to change it finally conclude that inadequate, slow, bulky, uncertain and in some instances corrupt and incompetent as it may be, it is still the best, most honest, and most efficient yet devised.

In a just trial under the jury system, three components of the tribunal are essential. The trial judge, the jury, and the attorneys. Each has a separate and important duty. In Massachusetts each must perform his part and generally speaking one cannot delegate that part to the other. 

II. The trial court-A. Generally. To procure justice the tribunal of trial must contain a directing mind; otherwise disorder and confusion would result. "The wise and impartial judge who discharges the duties of his office is the directing spirit, controlling mind and dominating force at the trial and acts to the end that a just result be reached." As such controlling spirit and directing mind, he faces in the course of a trial acts which he must perform and acts which he may perform; and there are a few acts which he must not perform.5 

In the admitting and excluding of evidence and in conduction of the hearing, if a fair trial is to be had, he must faithfully follow the material rules of law, must respect the rights of the jury and of parties, and their attorneys, and must faithfully and impartially assist in procuring a just verdict." B. The court must be impartial. "It is contrary to natural rights and fundamental principles of the common law for one to judge of his own cause."7 "'" A judge who is personally interested in the outcome of a case is barred from exercising any

Interested Judge:-The defendant was arrested for violation of the liquor laws of Ohio, and was tried before a justice of the peace, who had jurisdiction to try such cases without a jury. Ohio

D. The court must act judicially. "Parties are entitled to the exercise of the judicial faculty by the magistrate before whom a case is presented. Even a positive statement of intention by a party in the event of an adverse decision to take a case to another tribunal is no justification for a decision or ruling as a mere matter of form when a decision or ruling is required. 

A decision resting upon the application of sound learning and judicial experience may be accepted by a defeated party in the calmness of reflection even when a more captious attitude of mind precedes such decision. The purpose manifested by the organization of the several courts of this Commonwealth is that a decision should be made of each case on its merits by each tribunal before which it may come unless there is express provision of different nature." 22

2. Findings of preliminary questions of fact in civil casesa. Generally. When a preliminary finding of fact is essential to the admissibility of evidence in civil cases the court hears those facts, determines the truth and admits or excludes accordingly.26 The instance which furnishes the best illustration arises when the court is called on to pass on the admissibility of a statement of a deceased person under General Laws, chapter 233, section 65. That statute provides that any statement of fact made by a person deceased at the time of trial, of his own knowledge, in good faith, and before suit, is admissible. When testimony of such statement is offered, the court, and not the jury, determines its admissibility. To admit it the court must find that the statement was actually made, and that it is one of facts within the speaker's personal knowledge, made in good faith, and before suit started. The jury does not pass on these questions. If the judge decides that the statement was not made, or that the witness who now offers to testify to the statement did not hear it, or that any other condition imposed by the statute as a requisite of admissibility has not been proved, he must exclude the evidence, and his finding will not be readily disturbed.28 This illustrates the general principle as applied in

In criminal cases, at least to some extent, the rule is at variance. 88 b. The rule stated. When the admissibility of evidence in a civil case 29 depends on some preliminary finding of fact the court hears the evidence, preferably out of the hearing of the jury, determines what is the true situation,32 and admits or excludes the evidence accordingly; all presumptions are made in favor of the correctness of the court's finding 34 and his findings will not be readily disturbed.35 If he makes no express findings of fact, or if the bill of exceptions shows no such findings, it will be assumed that his admission or exclusion of evidence was proper and that he found preliminary facts requisite to admission or failed to find such preliminary facts, and acted accordingly. A party offering or objecting to evidence is entitled to an express finding on the required facts; 7 and if the court on due request fails to set out his findings of fact, an exception will lie.38 How specific these requests must be seems undecided, but doubtless the court may require the excepting party to point out what facts he relies on to establish admissibility, or what material fact he considers not established on that issue.89 36

3. Findings of preliminary questions of fact in criminal cases: The "humane practice"-a. Generally. In criminal cases by a long established custom, the rule as to the finality of the court's findings on preliminary questions of admissibility in certain instances has been varied and the jury is permitted to re-pass on admissibility. A statute which might have been interpreted as against this process has not changed the procedure.65 In such cases in the first instance the decision rests with the presiding judge. If he thinks that a confession or statement was not voluntary he excludes it and the matter is ended unless some question of law is raised 66 and his decision reversed. If the judge finds the facts which render the evidence admissible established, he admits the whole evidence.67 The jury re-hears the evidence on the preliminary matters and if they disagree with the result of the judge's finding on the preliminary questions of fact they treat the evidence as excluded.68 

It must be borne in mind that the trial judge must first pass on preliminary facts, he cannot delegate that duty to the jury.69 upon the ground of mental infirmity from age or any other cause. The court enumerates his qualifications as follows: (1) Residence in town where land to be valued was for sixty years; (2) 26 years of which a farmer; (3) traded in land in the town; (4) had seen the land in question; (5) knew its situation and general character; (6) somewhat acquainted with shooting in the vicinity; (7) had held important town offices; (8) as assessor at a time not remote had appraised the land; (9) "a typical islander of reliable character." Even though there is no offer of proof; the judge was wrong in excluding the evidence. Muskeget Island Club v. Nantucket, 185 Mass. 303.

Instances to which applicable (1) Generally. How far this "humane practice" is to be carried in criminal cases is not decided. Clearly it applies only to findings of fact on preliminary questions of evidence; it has nothing to do with matters involving "discretion." 78 These two principles,-findings of preliminary facts and discretion—are frequently confused; " in this instance to confuse them would lead to error. To extend the "humane practice" to all issues where preliminary questions of fact are involved would confuse the jury, prolong the trial, and draw much from the prestige of the trial judge. As the doctrine rested originally in consent 75 rather than in right, it need not be extended to all instances which involve preliminary questions. In some cases, however, the "humane practice" is established. (2) Confessions. The subject of confessions is considered elsewhere.76 Here we are concerned only with the judge's and jury's province in determining whether a confession was voluntary. As stated above the trial judge first must pass on this question. If he finds the confession involuntary he excludes it and there is the end. If he finds it voluntary he admits it, allows the jury to hear the evidence on the preliminary questions of fact, and instructs them to disregard the evidence if they do not find it voluntary; " the jury then finally decide the questions of fact which concern admissibility. Of course if there is no conflict as to the facts there is nothing for the jury to pass on; but "when there is conflicting testimony the humane practice. is for the judge if he considers that it is admissible to instruct 77

21 admissibility is to be passed on by the jury.84 The court in the following language has approved this proceeding. (4) Dying declarations. When a dying declaration is material and a proper subject for evidential purposes, to permit admissibility the existence of certain preliminary facts is necessary.⁹ 

7,90 Chief among these is the fact that the declarant at the time of his declaration had abandoned all hope of recovery, 91 and has died as a result of the injury then received.92 Other preliminary facts must be established, but these two are the most essential.98 The procedure is the same as in confessions.94 

First, the court passes on the preliminary facts. If he finds that any required preliminary fact is not established he excludes the declaration.95 If, on the other hand, he finds all necessary preliminary facts to be established he admits the declaration for the consideration of the jury, instructing them to consider the declaration as evidence of the truth of the statements therein, only if they find the preliminary facts to be proved, and to reject the evidence as of no probative value unless they so find.96 If the jury find the required preliminary facts established they consider the evidence and its weight.⁹7 

The court may tell the jury the reason for his admission of the evidence.98 The preliminary facts may be established by direct evidence, by statements of the deceased in the declaration, and by attending facts and circumstances.99 en them to consider the conversation as to identification only in the event that they should find that the defendant was not under arrest.'' 23 (5) Other instances. This principle of submitting to the jury the preliminary questions of admissibility should not be applied to every question of admissibility which arises on preliminary facts. So to apply it would confuse the jury, prolong argument of counsel, and break the prestige of the court.100 In confessions and dying declarations the procedure is established. 

High authority limits it to those two subjects. 101 In conspiracy, proof of the association of the conspirators is essential to proof of the offense and likewise to the admission of acts and words. of one conspirator as evidence against the other.10% In such cases the same procedure should be followed as in confessions and in dying declarations. The same is true when identity is involved.108 In other states it seems that the questions whether a preliminary matter of a privilege has been established,104 and whether a witness is disqualified by interest,105 are to be redecided by the jury. These courts have extended the rule to many other cases. 106 c. Probable rule. Perhaps the rule finally will be established to the effect that if the offered evidence goes to the vitals of the proof of guilt, and is admitted by the court, the jury will be allowed in all matters in criminal cases to re-pass on the preliminary facts before they consider the offered evidence of probative value.107 

4. Limitation of the rule. The decisions of the supreme judicial court repeatedly state that in civil actions the findings of fact on preliminary questions of admissibility, unless open under some process to be passed on by the higher court, are conclusive. This statement might lead to misunderstandings. Let us suppose that evidence of a statement of a deceased person is offered under the statute.110 To admit such statement in evidence the court must find among other preliminary facts that it was made in good faith and before suit brought.111 The court believes that the person alleged to have made the declaration had no reason to mis-state, that any statement that he might have made would be true and accurate, and that he saw the witness who now offers to repeat the statement only once and that before suit brought. The court, however, does not believe that the statement was ever made. If he cannot find that the statement was made, he cannot find that it was made in good faith, or before suit, hence he excludes it.112 Now contrast this case with an admission by a party. Let us assume that in a suit on a note, the signature is in issue. The plaintiff offers evidence that the defendant stated that the signature on the note was his and that he owed the note. The court finds that the witness did not know and could not identify the defendant,118 that the defendant at the time of the alleged statement was at a place or in a condition where he could not talk with the witness,114 or that though the witness knew and talked with the defendant the defendant never made the statement. May the court exclude this evidence?

Perhaps the question can be best answered after consideration of the history and reason for trial by jury. Trial by a judge

25 is much older than trial by jury. No one could question but that in formulating rules of law a judge or court of judges who give their lives to the study of laws is superior to a transient jury. Juries were not created to make laws. The function of the jury is to determine facts and in determining facts, first and foremost arises credibility of witnesses. It has been the belief of the people for centuries that a jury is the best judge of credibility. Credibility is for the jury.115 All matters strictly of fact which go to the merits are taken from the court and placed within the province of the jury. This includes credibility of witnesses. All other matters remain with the court.116 If a legitimate question of fact worthy of consideration goes to the merits, the jury should pass on it; but if it is not worthy of consideration the court should not allow it to be presented. If a preliminary question of fact is one purely of evidence except in unusual cases the court and not the jury finally passes on it; but if the preliminary question of fact goes also to the merits of the case and involves credibility, the court ordinarily will consider whether there is sufficient evidence to make it prima facie admissible.117 If then the evidence is directly to the issue and admissible within a well established exception of the rules of exclusion,118 in civil, but not in criminal cases he probably must admit it; 119 if on the other hand it is within the province of his discretion he may admit or exclude it; 120 but if it is made admissible by statute which requires certain preliminary findings he must exclude it unless he finds the preliminary requisites established.121 If the court on proper evidence finds the preliminary

184"Earnest argument has been addressed to us in behalf of the plaintiffs that the charge was open to exception in that it was argumentative and put emphasis upon inconsistencies in the testimony of the plaintiff, Buckley, without calling attention to inconsistencies in the testimony of the female defendant, these being the two witnesses upon whose testimony the verdict of the jury must be mainly founded. 

The duties of a judge presiding over a jury trial have been stated in several recent decisions. It was said in Whitney v. Wellesley & B. St. R. Co., 197 

Mass. 495, 502, 84 N. E. 95, with ample citation of authorities, that: The judge 'may sum up the testimony according to his recollection. 

In any clear analysis of the evidence, however impartial, the attention of the jury necessarily must be directed to the weight and importance of particular facts which they may find to have been proved. If an unbiased analytical statement of the testimony and of the law distinctly indicates the party who is entitled to prevail, this furnishes no just reason for the defeated party to complain, either of the method employed or of the adverse verdict. Besides, it is not a violation of the constitutional requirement that judges shall be as free, impartial and independent as the lot of humanity will admit, if the instructions, while judicially fair, are comprehensively strong, rather than hesitatingly barren or ineffective, and neither the tone of a charge not the form of verbal delivery are of themselves ground of exception, if no error of law appears. In a word, the judge who discharges the functions of his office is, under the statute as well as at common law, the directing and controlling mind at the trial, and not a mere functionary to preserve order and lend ceremonial dignity to the proceedings.' This principle has been amplified and applied in subse quent adjudications. Plummer v. Bos ton Elevated R. Co., 198 Mass. 499, 514, 515, 84 N. E. 849; Sawyer v. Worcester 

Consol. St. R. Co., 231 Mass. 215, 218, 219, 120 N. E. 404; Posell v. Herscovitz, 237 Mass. 513, 515, 130 N. E. 69; O'Neill v. Ross, 250 Mass. 92, 96, 97, 145 N. E. 

60; Field v. Hamm, 254 Mass. 268, 271, 150 N. E. 3. See also, State v. Moses, 13 N. C. 452, 456-463. We are of opinion that it cannot be said that there was failure of duty in this respect by the trial judge. It has not been argued that he did not correctly summarize the evidence of the witness Buckley. 

The complaint is that the judge made some calculations as to distance traveled by each motor vehicle in a given time based on that evidence, and then said: 'Is that probable, or is it probable that something may be the matter with Mr. Buckley's estimates somewhere, It is for you to say.

What are the facts? Is Mr. Buckley accurate when he states those distances and rates of speed? And that is for you to consider and determine, among other things.' 

There appears to us to be nothing

point out the importance of certain facts,185 and the reasons for the admissibility of evidence.186 The judge's tone of voice or verbal delivery is not subject for exception.187 He must not open to exception in this. The whole matter of speed was fairly left to the jury. The difficulties in the way of making accurate estimates of speed and distance by witnesses testifying long after the events were clearly set forth in the charge. The circumstance that no calculations as to speed and distance were made by the judge based on the testimony of the female defendant did not render the charge unfair. Her testimony does not seem to us readily susceptible of such analysis. However, that may be, the charge as an entirety appears to have left the negligence of both parties fairly to the jury. The contentions of each side were stated with sufficient reference to the evidence and facts to enable the jury to reach a correct decision. The charge does not seem to us indicative of any opinion by the judge as to the facts, nor to constitute a violation in any degree of the rights of the plaintiffs. 

A reading of the entire charge produces the conviction in our minds that it states fairly the respective contentions of the parties, and does not over emphasize one part of the evidence as compared with other parts, and does not disclose which witness seemed to the judge the more credible, or which party ought to prevail. It appears to us to be impartial and clear, and to do justice to both sides. Exceptions overruled." Buckley v. Frankel, 262 Mass. 13.

Separating single sentence from whole. It is settled that a single sentence or paragraph of a charge cannot be disconnected from the context, as ground for reversible error, if as a whole the instructions are correct. 

Maloy v. Boston Elevated, Feb. 27, 1914, 217 Mass. 108. Taken in connection with the entire charge to the jury held that there was no error in a statement therein, "A chisel or a stone bit, though a tool in common use has been stated by the Supreme Court to be as efficacious in the hands of a burglar to carry out his felonious intent as a jimmy or lock picker." Commonwealth v. Anderson, 245 Mass. 179. 

Instructions as to witnesses to be believed. The judge, in speaking of the evidence on the question of liability, used the expression, "see if there is anybody of whom you can say, 'I am convinced by that person,' and in discussing the testimony of the experts on the question of injury, the judge stated, "You may pick out one or two of those men that you say you will stand by." The tenor and purport of the entire charge were that the jury were to decide the case according to all the evidence, remembering that the burden of proof was upon the plaintiff to satisfy them on all the features of the case. The defendant alleged an exception "To so much of the charge as said that the jury should try to pick out one witness, because, it seems to neglect the question of weight of the evidence. Held, that, although taken by themselves, the expressions of the judge above quoted were objectionable, no substantial error appeared when the charge was considered as a whole. 

Cronin v. Boston Elevated, 233 Mass. 243.

What charge should contain. It is the duty of a persiding judge to state in his charge to the jury the principles of law applicable to the issues on trial, and it is within his province to state the testimony in his instructions fairly and impartially and to submit to the jury all questions of fact material to the issues in dispute without prejudice and without any attempt to influence their verdict. It was held that the judge clearly and accurately and with apt illustrations pointed out to the jury the duty which the defendant's motorman, in the operation and management of the car, owed to the plaintiff's intestate. Sawyer v. Worcester 

Com., 231 Mass. 215.

Using illustrations in charge: A presiding judge may use illustrations for the purpose of more pointedly directing the attention of the jury to the questions they are to decide. This is a matter of discretion, not to be reviewed unless prejudicial error positively is shown; and none was held to have been shown in the present case. Draper v.

V. 

Necessity of calling attention to error. The defendant contended that the judge had given an instruction which authorized the jury to find that the driver was acting within the scope of his employment, without considering the effect of ratification and express approval, but it appeared that the defendant did not call the attention of the judge to this objection to the instruction given by him, and took no specific exception to any part of the judge's charge. Held, that the contention, whether warranted by anything in the charge or not was not open to the defendant. O'Neil v. National Oil Co., 231 Mass. 20. 

Failure to direct Judge's attention to specific matters: The judge instructed the jury fully as to the law upon the main issues presented, to which no exception was taken. The charge contained no reference to the alleged larceny of brass. The defendant did not make any request that an instruction should be given on that subject, did not call the judge's attention to the omission of the subject from the charge, and saved no exception on the subject. Held, that it was not open to the defendant to contend in this court that the omission of instructions on the subject of larceny of the brass was error entitling him to a new trial. 

Commonwealth v. Feci, 235 Mass. 563. (This case is to be noted with care. 

Failure to except had a direct bearing on a man's execution.)

The defendant asked for an instruction to the effect that the plaintiff could not recover unless there was an agreement between the defendant and the deceased "to make repairs, negligent making of them, and an injury to her in consequence of such gross negligence."

This was not correct as to the death count, but it was sound as to the count for conscious suffering. It was enough to call the attention of the judge to the matter of gross negligence. He, however, made no distinction in his charge and instructed the jury that if the defendant "undertook to make repairs in a gratuitous way for the wife, and he assured her the premises were safe after he made them, and she was injured as a result of negligence in making the repairs, even though gratuitously undertaken, she may recover unless you find she was not in the exercise of due care. In this there was error. As the judge should have drawn the distinction between the degree of negligence which would warrant recovery in the count for death and for conscious suffering, exceptions on that point must be sustained. Even though the request was not strictly accurate in the general form in which it was presented, it was sufficient to direct the consideration of the judge to an important principle of law not adverted to in the charge, an omission of which well may have resulted in harm to the defendant. (Citing, Bride v. Clark, 161 Mass. 130;

Yancye v. Boston El. Ry., 205 Mass. 

162, 172; Gascoigne v. Cary Brick Co., 217 Mass. 302, 305.) Bergeron v. Forest, 233 Mass. 392 at 402.

Requests not applicable to facts: 

The judge need not give ruling, that, "there is no absolute rule of law that a person driving across a street in a city, in crossing the tracks of a street railway in a public street where the cars have not an exclusive right of way must look and listen for an approaching car before entering upon the tracks of the electric railway.

Even if it is a correct statement of the law especially where it appears that the driver of the plaintiff's team testified that he did look for a car before crossing the defendant's tracks and did not see one until it was six feet from him the court must not give it. McNeil v. Middlesex & Boston Street Ry., 233 Mass. 254. 

Proper to refuse to grant rulings of law, correct as abstract propositions, if there is no issue at the trial to which they are applicable. Judge who has instructed a jury fully as to principles of law applicable at a trial, properly may refuse to grant requests which single out certain portions of the evidence and ask for rulings as to their effect. Director General of R. R. v. 

Eastern S. S. Lines, 245 Mass. 387. 

Request for inapplicable ruling: A request for an instruction to the jury stating a sound principle of law which is not applicable to the evidence is refused properly. Duart v. Simmons, 231 

Mass. 314.

Reading to jury requests and commenting on them: An exception to the conduct of the judge in reading to the jury at the close of his charge requests previously presented to him by one of the parties, with comments upon them as he read them, instead of covering the subject matter of the requests in the course of his charge, was overruled. Maryland Casualty Co. v. Jackson et al., 230 Mass. 384. 

Shaking head during argument of counsel: If the judge at a trial during the course of the closing argument of the counsel for the plaintiff by motions of his head shows dissent from the counsel's statements and the plaintiff does not except to such conduct of the judge before the verdict, the propriety of such conduct cannot be brought before this court for determination by an exception to a refusal to grant a motion for a new trial based upon such alleged impropriety. Murray v. Liebmann, 231

See the following particularly as to immediate notice. The phrase in section four: "In event of accidental death immediate notice thereof must be given to the Association" is to be read with the provision of section five that "Failure to give notice within the time provided in this policy shall not invalidate any claim if it shall be shown not to have been reasonably possible to give such notice," and as so read the question of "immediate notice" is a question of due diligence in sending the notice with reasonable promptness in the circumstances of each case. (Citing 

Everson v. General Accident, Fire & Life 

Assurance Corp., Ltd., 202 Mass. 169, 174; 88 N. E. 658, Greenough v. Phoenix 

Ins. Co. of Hartford, 206 Mass. 247, 249, 92 N. E. 447, 138 Am. St. Rep. 383, and cases cited.) The context in which the words "immediate notice" occur in this policy is of weight in ascertaining their signification. Manifestly they are used in contradistinction to the time within which notice of other claims must be given. In case of disability arising from accident, the notice must be given within twenty days after the accident; in case of disability arising from sickness, the notice must be given within ten days after the commencement of the disability; but in case of accidental death "immediate notice" must be given. This arrangement of words and this specification of times seem to emphasize the requirement of promptness in giving the death notice. Brief periods of definite days are agreed upon with respect to the time for giving the other two notices, but the notice of death must be "immediate." That word in such connection can mean only that the notice must be sent quickly, with dispatch, with speed. Wilcox v.

R. 861, as follows:-"Limitation of Action-Computation of Time-Inclusion and Exclusion of First and Last Days.-By a deed executed on April 14, 1902, the defendant granted a period of ten years in which to cut and remove timber from his land. The deed also provided that if such timber were not removed at the expiration of the ten years the grantee was to have the option of extending the period. On April 15, 1912, April 14 having fallen on Sunday, the plaintiff, a mesne grantee, gave notice of his desire to extend. Held, that the option was exercised in time. United 

Timber Co. v. Bivins, 253 Fed. 968.

As a general rule, in the computation of time from a date or an event, the first day is excluded and the last in-

by statute or contract falls on Sunday or a legal holiday, unless it is specifically authorized or required to be performed on Sunday or on a legal holiday, the act may be performed on the next succeeding business day.289 It is well to note the attitude of the law of equity toward considering "time of the essence.' 

Equity in this respect in matters which do not involve an option tends towards holding time of the essence only when it is excluded. Blake v. Crowninshield, 9 N. 

H. 304; Seward v. Hayden, 150 Mass. 

158, 22 N. E. 629; McCulloch v. Hopper, 47 N. J. L. 189. Some courts hold, however, adopting an old common-law distinction, that where the period is to be reckoned from an event, as distinguished from a date, both days are to be included. Bellasis v. Hester, 1 

Ld. Raym. 280; Chiles v. Smith, 52 Ky. 

460; Leavenworth Coal Co. v. Barber, 47 Kan. 29, 27 Pac. 114. On the other hand, to prevent hardship or forfeiture, the general rule has often been discarded, the first and last days being included or excluded as the case required. Lester v. Garland, 15 Ves. 248; 

Pugh v. Duke of Leeds, Cowp. 714; 

Price v. Whitman, 8 Cal. 417; Taylor v. Brown, 5 Dak. 335, 40 N. W. 525.

The law is even more uncertain when the last day falls on Sunday. With respect to contracts the Sunday is generally excluded, and performance may properly occur on Monday. Campbell v. Life Assurance Society, 41 Bosw. 

299; Hammond v. Life Ins. Co., 10 

Gray (Mass.) 306; Everett v. Stewart, 2 Conn. 69. But in the computation of statutory periods there can be no extension of time. Alderman v. Phelps, 15 Mass. 225; Patrick v. Faulke, 45 Mo. 

312; Harrison v. Sager, 27 Mich. 476. 

Contra, West v. West, 20 R. I. 464, 40

Atl. 6. Statutes providing for the exclusion of Sunday have changed the latter rule in many jurisdictions.

U. S. Rev. Stat. section 5013; N. Y. 

Code Civ. Proc. section 788; Ky. Civ.

Code Prac., section 681. But curiously, these statutes have been considered as requiring performance on Saturday instead of permitting an extension until the following Monday. Frankfort v. 

Farmers' Bank, 20 Ky. L. 1635, 49 S. 

W. 811; Allen v. Elliott, 67 Ala. 432.

Again, it has been held that these stat- 

utes have no application where the period in question covers a number of years. Williams v. Lane, 87 Wis. 152, 58 N. W. 77; Haley v. Young, 144 Mass. 

364. The many fine-spun distinctions drawn by the courts relative to this question seem unjustifiable. Computation of time is a matter purely of technical construction, and no reason appears why a definite principle should not be formulated to apply equally to all cases. The rights and liabilities of parties with respect to a matter which So often leads to important consequences should be fixed and certain.

"Torts-Malicious Prosecution-Compromise of Pros ecution as Bar to Action.-The defend ant instituted a prosecution against the plaintiff for obtaining goods by means of a worthless check. On the warrant issued was an indorsement directing the officer executing it to accept payment of the bill and costs, if the plaintiff would pay. The officer presented the warrant to the plaintiff, and told him that he was under arrest. The plaintiff, to avoid going to jail, paid the bill and costs, and was released. 

A nolle prosequi was subsequently entered. The plaintiff later brought an action for malicious prosecution and was non-suited on the above evidence. 

He appealed. Held, that the entry of nolle prosequi, and the plaintiff's discharge was such a termination of the prosecution as would enable the plaintiff to maintain this action; and that if the object of the prosecution was to collect the defendant's claim, this fact was evidence of malice. As a matter of law one who acts with probable cause in instituting criminal process is not liable in malicious prosecution though he acts with malice 269 and the jury should be instructed that if the defendant made a full and fair disclosure of facts known to him, to the police and left them to take the proper course without pressure or coercion he is not liable.270

If no facts warrant a finding of these two essentials the court rules that the plaintiff cannot recover,274 but when the evidence warrants a finding for the plaintiff the court will submit the case with instructions as to inferences and presumptions of fact to the jury.275 Probable cause when all these instructions are given is one of fact.276 Of course questions of what the governing law was in the action which is alleged to have been prosecuted maliciously and without probable cause, is a question for the court and as to that he will instruct the jury.277

Q. Judicial notice 1. Generally. Two classes of facts are noted without judicial proof,-those which fall within judicial notice and those which fall within common knowledge.295 The former includes some established matters, knowledge of which is general among studious and enlightened people and is acquired by specific study; the latter includes matters which are known generally by the average reasonable man of the community where the case is tried. The first are noted without proof by the court who expounds them to the jury; 296 the latter are noted by the jury without proof. 

2. Distinguished from other matters-a. Common knowledge. Judicial notice as said above is to be distinguished from common knowledge. The former applies to matters of a judicial nature, those which involve questions of the arts and sciences, and those which involve a deeper study than need be applied to learn matters of common knowledge. Common knowledge comprises that knowledge of facts and the relationship of fact to fact, and cause to result, which is picked up and retained by the ordinary reasonably observant man in the ordinary course of ordinary experience in the community of trial.297 b. Judge's private knowledge-(1) Duty of judge to testify. A judge's private knowledge of facts is not to be noted by judicial notice.298

Before hearing this motion the court evidently desired to know the width of the platform; and at the request of the court one Witkins a civil engineer testified that he had measured the platform, and he gave the distances. 

These seem to have been substantially embodied in the record as the true measurements. These measurements having been put in, "upon the further request of the court that before argument of the question of law, testimony be introduced as to the amount of overhang of the locomotive which struck the plaintiff, the defendant introduced testimony that the beam of the engine which struck the plaintiff projected 22 inches beyond the inside of the rail, and that the cylinder of the same engine projected 22½ inches beyond the inside of the rail." The defendant was not requested to rest before arguing its motion to direct a verdict for the defendant, and did not rest. "Upon this record it is plain that both court and counsel understood that the question upon which the defendant desired to be heard was the one subsequently formally presented, namely that upon all the evidence the plaintiff was not entitled to recover; that in order to rule intelligently upon that question the presiding judge wanted some more definite information as to the dimensions. This further testimony was introduced. After it was put in the plaintiff made no effort to contradict it, nor does it appear that in arguing the questions of law he in any way disputed the measurements. All parties must have understood that this evidence was put in not merely for the

d. Right to call and examine witnesses. A trial judge has the right to call and to examine witnesses,805 but the testimony thus disclosed is not to be given any greater weight than it would have received had either party called and examined the witness. If the court examines a witness the necessity of objection and exception may be removed.806 

3. As to the court's duty to take judicial notice: Necessity of request. The question of the court's obligations on its own motion to take judicial notice is one which recently has become more practical. A statute which requires the court to take judicial notice of laws of certain other jurisdictions is the cause.807 Does this statute mean that in a case which depends on the interpretation of foreign law, after all evidence has been presented, the court may surprise both parties by telling the jury that a statute of the foreign jurisdiction controls, read to them the statute, and expound its meaning? Does it mean that he must do so? Does it mean that after the facts are ascertained and the case is pending on exceptions, the full bench may reverse a decision because in its study it has found a statute or a decision of a foreign jurisdiction, unknown to either party, which it believes governs the case? 

It is said that the court is not obliged to note facts judicially 808 That his doing so is discretionary, and that an attorney who desires that facts be noted judicially should outline the facts to be noted and request that the court note them. Customary courtesy seems to have borne out this assumption. 

Usually an attorney in asking the court to take judicial notice of a matter, presents to the court the authoritative statement of which he wishes notice taken. If he fails to make any request purpose of being weighed against any measurement made by the plaintiff, be- cause the plaintiff had made none; nor even vaguely to contradict the vague evidence of the plaintiff on this matter, but to settle all questions as to these distances and that they be taken as facts by the presiding judge in considering the general questions of law to be argued before him. Under these circumstances it was the duty of the plaintiff to make known his intention to dispute the accuracy of the testimony. The rule applied in Lindenbaum v. New York, New Haven & Hartford 

Railroad, 197 Mass. 314, 323, is not applicable." Hutcheson v. B. & M., 219 

Mass. 389.

Evidence Judicial notice Interpre tation of statute requiring judicial notice of foreign law.—A statute required the courts to take judicial notice of the laws of other states. Mass. Laws 1926, c. 168. The plaintiff sued on a judgment obtained in 1927 in the supreme court of New York. A New York statute provided that an action upon a judgment rendered in a court of record of 

New York cannot be maintained unless ten years have elapsed since the docketing of such judgment. N. Y. C. P. A. (1921) section 484. Judgment was given for the plaintiff. On appeal the defendant asked for the first time that the court take judicial notice of this statute. Held, that the New York statute is a statute of limitations and must be pleaded specially, and that since it was not called to the attention of the trial court it cannot be considered on appeal. Further discussion.

There was no jury involved in the Lennon case but the court's remarks about foreign law as a 'question of fact' with references to Wylie v. Cotter, and Electric Welding Co. v. Prince, which were the very cases that led to the enactment of the statute, seem somewhat ambiguous in view of the previous recognition of the statute by the court referred to in the note above quoted.

The late James B. Thayer pointed out that foreign law was no more a question of fact than domestic law and

cedure on exceptions.310 If the court does note a fact which is legally within judicial notice, without request, has the adversary a right on exceptions? No. The court of its own motion without request, during trial, apparently may note facts judicially.811

The proper procedure then seems to be for the attorney who desires the court to note a fact judicially to request such notice, and courtesy requires that he furnish the court with the authentic material information.812 Though certain facts might be that when what was wanted was 'the rule or law of the case' the same sort of question is presented whether the law be domestic or foreign, and that the question should in all cases be answered by the judge. 'The circumstance that while the domestic law does not need to be proved by evidence, strictly so-called, foreign law must be so proved, is not material. 

In reason the judges might well enough be allowed to inform themselves about foreign law in any manner they choose, just as the judges of the Federal Court notice without proof the laws of all the states. But if it is required to be proved, it should be proved to the judge.'

Preliminary treatise on evidence, pp. 257-8. Dean Wigmore supports these views. Wigmore on Evidence, Volume IV, Secs. 2549, 2558. 

Sections 5726 and 5727 of the Connecticut General Statutes, Revision of 1918. 

Sec. 5726. Printed statutes of other states. The public statutes of the several states and territories in the United States as printed by authority of the state or territory exacting the same and the private or special acts of this state shall be legal evidence and the courts shall take judicial notice of them. 

Sec. 5727. Reports of judicial decisions of other states. The reports of the judicial decisions of other states and countries may be judicially noticed by the courts of this state as evidence of the common law of such states or countries and of the judicial construction of the statutes or other laws thereof. Cf. Hale v. N. J. Steam Nav. Co., 15 Conn. 539 (1843); Lockwood v. 

Crawford, 18 Conn. 361 (1847).

A similar act appears in the New Jersey compiled Statutes, Vol. 2, p. 2228. For further discussion see Massachusetts Law Quarterly for August, 

We think a careful tracing of the history of the earlier Massachusetts rule that questions of law were questions of fact to be decided by a jury will show that it developed gradually as a result of misunderstanding of certain passages in opinions about a century ago. A rule thus developed can surely be changed by statute. We have not these opinions at hand at the moment but will discuss the matter further in a later issue. It would seem that a question of law, foreign or domestic, is not and never has been, except by local judicial definition, a question of fact of the character for the decision of which jury trial was provided. As pointed out by Prof. Thayer and others, it has never been the law that every question of fact which may arise in a case must be decided by a jury. The very phrase 'to take judicial notice' illustrates this. A local judicial definition which discriminates between the nature of a question of Massachusetts law and a question of Connecticut or New York law does not seem to be beyond legislative modification by the extension of the scope of judicial notice."

61 experts,101 and when no oral testimony or written decisions were in evidence, on the interpretation of written statutes.402 The trial judge was not to carry at all times a knowledge of all law.403 To carry even the law of the forum seemed to at least one judge an unbearable burden. In speaking of the much quoted by-word "all men are taken to know the law," that humane jurist, with a zeal that showed something of humorous and sympathetic pity, punctuates his decision with the expression, "God forbid that it should be imagined that an attorney or a counsel, or even a judge is bound to know all the law." 404 The legislature has not heeded the prayer. By acts of 1926, chapter 168, it has provided that the "courts shall take judicial notice of the law of the United States or of any state, territory or dependency thereof, or of a foreign country whenever the same shall be material." 405 The statute does not limit this judicial knowledge to matters of substantive law,408 nor expressly to matters of public law.407 This statute apparently includes, when the questions are properly raised, matters of procedure.408 If the clause "whenever the same shall be material" means that the court shall of its own motion note such law without the request or assistance of counsel,409 it constitutes a wide departure. If that clause signifies that failure to ask the court to take judicial notice of foreign law renders such judicial notice not "material," 410 then the burden on the court is less and the dangers of surprise are reduced. (2) In other states. In other jurisdictions judicial notice includes a wide range. R. To exercise a wise discretion-1. Introductory: Discre tion distinguished from preliminary findings of fact. In many matters a trial court has discretionary power.476 In the exercise of that power he will not be overruled unless his decision is clearly wrong.477 He is in the atmosphere of the trial; he therefore can judge better of the justice of a specific discretionary ruling than an appellate court.478 

Discretion is frequently confused with findings on questions of fact preliminary to admissibility.479 They are to be distinguished. On questions of admissibility when preliminary facts are to be found the court must hear the material evidence offered to establish or to refute those facts, determine the truth of the evidence and make his findings.480 He has no "discretion" in making his findings. He cannot in his discretion disregard a fact which he has found to be established, and he cannot in his discretion refuse to consider a material fact which is established as true. His discretion extends to the admissibility state of the assets and liabilities of this trust company. If, and so far as, that is of any consequence, other proceedings have shown with seeming conclusiveness that it is hopelessly insolvent. It would be closing our eyes to the obvious to proceed on any other footing." Cosmopolitan Trust Co. v. Suffolk Knitting Mills, 247 Mass. 530.

THE COURT 

69 1 of certain kinds of evidence. In other classes of evidence on questions of admission or exclusion he has no discretion. These are the classes which go directly to the issue such as direct admissions and direct confessions, and lie within the clearly established exceptions to the rules of exclusion.481 Roughly speaking when the evidence offered is remote,182 far fetched,488 misleading,484 and not the "best" evidence,485 the court in admitting or excluding it has a limited discretion. This question is taken up in the discussion of each of the exceptions to the rules of exclusion in Part III, and in the consideration of the examination of witnesses in Part VI. It is well here to point out the more common instances wherein the court has and has not discretion in the admission and exclusion of evidence and in other matters, from the point of view of the general duties of the presiding officer at the trial, of the parties, and of their attorneys. 

2. Uniformity of rulings. "Discretion" does not imply an arbitrary power.486 The trial court must exercise a "sound judicial" discretion.487 As this is a government of laws and not of men,488 discretion under the same circumstances always should be exercised in the same way. 489 

3. The rule. The court has expressed the rule in substantially the following language. "It is the general rule that matters which rest in the judicial discretion of the trial court cannot be reviewed by this court. That question most frequently arises upon motions for new trials or to set aside verdicts. But the same principle applies broadly to discretionary rulings. It finds illustrations in orders as to filing further answers to inter-

71 (2) Limits of discretion-(a) Generally. A court's discretion in granting or refusing a new trial is wide. The exercise of his discretion will not be disturbed unless there is an error of law.498 If his decision can be supported on any ground,unless there is such ruling that it could not have been made in good faith, his decision will stand.499 To override his decision, discretion must have been abused and in his ruling on the motion, the record must show an error of law.500 (b) Must be on motions in civil matters. A court cannot now in civil actions set aside a verdict of a jury and grant a new trial "except on written motion by a party to the cause, stating the reasons relied upon in its support, filed and heard after notice to the adverse party according to the rules of the court.", 501 (c) If for excessive damages: Remittitur. A verdict shall not be set aside as excessive until the prevailing party has first been given an opportunity to remit so much thereof as the court adjudges is excessive.502 If it appears from the judge's statement filed in the case that a new trial is granted solely because damages were excessive, the new trial shall be confined solely to the question of damages.508 This is not to be confused with the court's right to correct an error of law with the consent of the jury; by statute the right to correct such errors may be asked of and received from the jury.504 (d) Justice granting new trial must state grounds. No new trial shall be granted for error in the admission or exclusion of evidence or for matter of pleading or procedure unless the justice before whom the question arises is satisfied that the error has affected substantial rights of the parties.506

Evidence of little probative value admitted wrongfully. The superintendent 

Williamson, testified that no foreman discharged employees without consulting him. The plaintiff testified that the foreman discharged him, saying, "Mr. Williamson told me to let you go.' Inadmissible demand by sheriff. In a civil case heard by the court without a jury a new trial may be the defendant; there was evidence of an understanding that the execution would not be served until a date to which plaintiff had requested that his possession might be extended; the defendant did not contest such proceedings; admission of the evidence was not harmful to the defendant. Warning to look out. "Look out for the cars" said to plaintiff by man on team with him, is excluded. Error is harmless because plaintiff already testified that he was looking out for the cars. Nathan v. Boston Elevated, 229

Excluding technical terms. At a trial of an action at tort, where the plaintiff sought to establish that certain material conduct of his occurred while he was in an unconscious or semi-unconscious condition following a fall in which he struck his head on a railroad track, there was evidence warranting a finding that he suffered the blow in the circumstances described and thereafter lost his "mind altogether, everything," and a medical expert was permitted to state that in his opinion the plaintiff's "unconsciousness was the result of his fall," that the blow to which he testified might cause him to be dazed, so as "not to be conscious of his surroundings, and that in that condition of loss of memory he could arise and carry his bundles. The expert also was permitted to testify at length as to the nature of a concussion of the brain. 

Certain further hypothetical questions of the medical expert, which related to whether the plaintiff's condition was due to a concussion of the brain, were excluded subject to exceptions by the plaintiff. Held, that (1) The probability of the plaintiff's story could not be materially increased by designating the mental condition from which he suffered as one of concussion of the brain rather than of dizziness, loss of memory, or unconsciousness; (2) The plaintiff was not harmed by the exclusion of the questions; (3) The exceptions must be overruled." Miller v. B. & M., 240 

Mass. 461. 

Letter contradictory of evidence and claim. Letter of defendant to plaintiff contained a provision not in the sales note, that "the delivery would have to be strictly subject to the arrival of our own importations, was excluded.

The defendant first relied on this provision in defense by an amended answer filed at the time of the trial of the action. Previous to that time, he had contended that no contract was made with the plaintiff. It appeared that the defendant never attempted to place an order for importation of burlap to fill the plaintiff's order, that it would have been impossible to procure importations to fulfil the requirements of the sale as to delivery unless the orders had been placed long before the contract with the plaintiff was made, and that the defendant did not rely on its own importations to fulfil the plaintiff's orders. Held, that exclusion of the letter did not harm the defendant in this respect. Wonalancet Co. v. Collins, 

Plass, Thayer Co., 234 Mass. 427.

Answer rendering admission of incompetent question harmless. Indictment charging that the defendant falsely testified that he did not own certain real estate; the defendant testified in his own behalf and, subject to his exception, was compelled to answer in cross-examination questions as to whether he had consulted a certain attorney at law with reference to disposing of his interest in the real estate and whether he had not said to the attorney that he wanted to get rid of his interest therein. His answer in substance was that he did not remember and that he "did not have any interest to say such a thing.' " Held, that the exceptions must be overruled because under the circumstances the defendant had no valid ground for complaint. Commonwealth v. Barronian, 235 Mass. 364. See Koplan v. Boston 

Gas Light Co., 177 Mass. 15; Manly v. 

Bay State St. Ry., 220 Mass. 124. The defendant Dies on cross examination was asked, "Didn't you have something to do with him (Lawyer Sullivan of Middleboro) before you were ar-

granted upon motion for a mistake of law or for newly disrested about this case?" and he answered, "Not before I was ar rested." No further questions were put in this regard. The defendant could not have been harmed. The exception must be overruled. Commonwealth v. Dies, Andrews, Gomes, 248 Mass. 482.

Request immaterial on the facts as found. An exception to a refusal of a request for a ruling that the plaintiff should be compelled to repay sum paid by the plaintiff out of money advanced for commissions, must be overruled where the judge who heard the case made a finding, without a report of the evidence, from which it clearly appeared that no money was advanced by the defendant on the mortgages involved in the suit. Dans v. Tremont 

Trust Co., 234 Mass. 503.

Verdict or invalid count rendering error immaterial. In an action to recover the purchase price paid for a bowling alley, where the judge rules that the case could not be submitted to the jury on the ground, relied on by the plaintiff, of rescission of the sale, it was held that certain requests for rulings made by the defendant relative to the plaintiff's right of rescission were rendered immaterial and properly were refused.

Requests for rulings based upon a count in declaration which is not submitted to the jury rightly may be refused as irrelevant.

An error in a charge to the jury which relates to damages for breach of an express or implied warranty of title is rendered immaterial by a verdict manifestly based upon the theory that no title passed to the plaintiff. Marciniak v. Walz, 239 Mass. 259. See also

Jury, Chapter 11. 

Error cured by verdict. Where, in an action of tort for the causing of conscious suffering and death through negligence, the jury found for the defendant, the plaintiff was not harmed by a refusal to grant a request for a ruling relating merely to the bearing of certain recited evidence upon the ascertainment of the degree of culpability of the defendant, which was the measure of damages under the count for the causing of death. Walsh v. Adams, 245 

Mass. 1. See Ch. II, numbers 675, 676, 677, 678. 

Admission of incompetent question rendered immaterial on special finding. 

Privileged matters. It is now argued that the alleged warning testified to in the answer occurred in a private conversation between husband and wife, although that objection was not raised at the trial. Assuming, however, that the answer was incompetent, and that the objection is now open to the plaintiff, it can not avail her in view of the special answer of the jury, that the chauffeur was not negligent. The evidence could bear only on the plaintiff's due care. Gillet v. Shaw, 217 

Mass. 59.

Verdict curing error. In cases tried together, it was held, that questions relating to the admission of evidence in regard to the title of the respective plaintiffs to the property damaged by fire, each of whom contended that the property belonged to him and not to the other plaintiff, had been made immaterial by the finding that the damage was not caused by the defendant. Bradford v. B. & M. Railroad, 225 Mass. 129. 

Bills and notes,-Record fails to show wrongfully admitted evidence of demand, harmless; no way to tell that it was disregarded. Simmons v. Poole, 227 Mass. 29.

Recovery on one count only could be sustained. Judge refuses to order verdict on other count. Harmless error.

Error cured by later instructions. 

Exceptions to the admission of immaterial evidence will not be sustained, where it appears that the judge instructed the jury in substance that he should have excluded the evidence and the exceptions were not argued by the excepting party in this court. Mercier v. Union St. Ry. Co., 234 Mass. 85.

Such later instructions must be clear, unequivocal and explicit. At the close of his charge to the jury, the presiding judge stated, "The fact that the defendant did not maintain a fence between the inward and outward bound tracks cannot be considered as evidence of negligence at that time."

Held, that this instruction was not sufficient in form to eradicate from the minds of the jury the effect, prejudicial to the defendant, of the evidence improperly admitted. It also was stated that in order to cure the error in the admission of the evidence above described, the judge should have instructed the jury to disregard for any purpose of proof, the fact that a fence had been erected by the defendant between the tracks after the accident. 

Conry v. Boston & Maine R. R., 227 Mass. 411. 

A clear, unequivocal and explicit instruction to disregard the evidence as incompetent usually cures the error. 

Where at a trial of an action of tort evidence is offered by the plaintiff, against the objection of the defendant, of certain matters for which the plaintiff claims damages; and the evidence, subject to the defendant's exception is admitted, but afterwards the presiding judge tells the jury to disregard this evidence, and again in his charge instructs them that the plaintiff can recover nothing for such matters, the rights of the defendant are protected fully, and his exception to the admission of the evidence cannot be sustained, because, if the evidence were admitted erroneously, the jury must have understood clearly that it was not to be considered. Mikkelson v. Connolly, 229 Mass. 360. 

Curing erroneous charge as to burden of proof. Error of court in will contest in instructing that contestant must prove undue influence beyond a reasonable doubt was corrected, when the judge said to the jury, "You have got to prove enough by way of fact, so that a reasonable inference that the will of the person has been overcome is properly drawn from the testimony," 

etc. Ceregheno v. Grannone, 247 Mass. 

319. 

Erroneous comment on facts. Unnecessary to determine whether the judge's comments on the testimony of the plaintiff's expert witness constituted error; as any prejudice created thereby was removed by the closing words of the charge. Henry J. Perkins 

Co. v. City of Springfield, 248 Mass. 447. 

Attorney's duty when error corrected. "The erroneous statement thus removed did not affect injuriously any statement allowed to remain. The exception must be overruled."'

Burden of showing error and harm on exceptions,-Failure to call trial court's attention to error. This has been held in general to be a constitutional regulation of the right of a trial by jury and not an impairment of its essential characteristics.546 The meaning of that part of the statute which makes imperative a hearing upon the written motion has not been declared by the court. By fair implication, that part of the statute enjoins that opportunity for reasonable argument be afforded to the party against whom the decision is made. As thus interpreted, the statute does not violate the constitutional right of trial by jury.' 547 Though as suggested above a person who has received a verdict is entitled to be heard before that verdict is set aside, yet this right is subject to regulation and may be lost by his inactivity or delay. The rule of court, therefore, referred to in the preceding section 548 which requires that this motion be presented to the trial judge within a limited time is valid.549 

The plea of unconstitutionality frequently is based on the sanctity of a verdict and the lack of power of a judge to override that verdict. A verdict, however, has not absolute sanctity if it is against the law. Hence if a plaintiff has a verdict and the trial judge, subject to exceptions, sets it aside and grants a new trial, though a verdict on the second trial is for the defendant, yet the exceptions of the plaintiff may be sustained and the first verdict may stand; the second verdict then is void.5

When exceptions are taken to the court's ruling unless the record shows error, the exceptions will not be sustained.574 All presumptions are made in favor of the court's ruling and his exercise of this discretionary power will not be overruled unless that power clearly has been abused.575 If the court in the "statement" required by statute sets out his findings of fact and other matters which pertain to his rulings, then if the statement is made part of the bill of exceptions it will be considered as part of the record.578 The proper procedure on hearing on such motion, particularly when the motion rests on new matter discovered or arising after the case went to the jury,577 seems to be to ask for specific findings of fact, or at least that the court set forth the facts found by him on specific issues.578 The moving party on a motion based on newly discovered facts should request a finding that the facts as found by him would in his opinion require a different verdict or would so seriously affect the result of the trial that the verdict rendered without their consideration is not a fair verdict. Statutes, however, have clarified this right.592 If a verdict is set aside because the damages are excessive the new trial is confined to the issue of damages; 598 but a verdict may be shown a compromise verdict by the inadequacy of damages, and if set aside as such compromise verdict, the whole issue should be retried.594 

When the court in setting aside a verdict legally orders that a new trial be confined to certain issues the new trial of course is confined to those issues 595 and evidence must be material on those issues to be admissible. If a verdict is set aside in the court's discretion without a positive ruling of law, and a new trial ordered without limitation as to issues the whole case is retried and evidence is admissible or inadmissible regardless of the previous trial. Such in all cases of new trials granted by the trial court is generally assumed to be the law. Whether the "law of the case" can affect this is arguable.
