THE COURT 

89 597 "law of the case" and on a second trial after a verdict is set aside, must the trial court on the same evidence order a verdict? 

In other words, if the court on a motion to set aside a verdict for the plaintiff on the ground that the verdict is against the evidence, erroneously grants the motion, is his ruling that the evidence is not sufficient to go to the jury, the law of the case; and if the same evidence and no more is again presented at a retrial, must the trial court direct a verdict for the defendant? 

Such should not be the law. However, if the Supreme Judicial court has ruled that the evidence in a case is not sufficient to carry it to the jury, on retrial if no further evidence is presented the trial court must order a verdict for the defendant.598 Were the question on which the trial court passed merely one of discretion and not of law, even though discretion always should be exercised in the same manner," 599 doubtless the "law of the case" would not bar a party from a full retrial without restriction which originated from the original trial. 

The right to order a new trial is not restricted to one such order. Repeated new trials may be ordered until justice is accomplished.000

By statute,601 the court may ask the jury's permission to enter a final judgment contrary to its verdict if as a matter of law such judgment should have been entered as a result of the trial. 

If the jury grants this right fatal error may be corrected by a final order without a retrial. This statute is constitutional.602

"At the trial of an action against an indorser of a promissory note, there was a verdict for the plaintiff. The defendant moved for a new trial on the ground that there was no evidence of notice to the defendant of non-payment of the note or of a waiver of such notice and stated to the court in substance that, if the motion was denied, exceptions would be taken. The motion was denied and no notice of such action was sent to the defendant. Judgment was entered for the plaintiff. The defendant thereupon filed a petition to vacate the judgment. Held, that (1) The petition disclosed ground which, as a matter of law, would not warrant a vacation of the judgment; (2) The question raised on the motion for a new trial should have been raised at the trial, when it would have been appropriate for the defendant to save an exception to an adverse ruling; (3) While the motion for a new trial might have been granted, the petitioner could not require it as a matter of right; (4)

common law set the methods by which he must protect himself against error.612 If he does not protect himself thus, he cannot complain if the court refuses to retry his case.618 Hence, that a party without valid excuse did not object and except to a remark of the trial judge,614 or to a question asked the jury by the trial judge,615 or to a refusal to grant a motion for a directed verdict,616 or to the inconsistency of the verdict with the charge,617 or to the insufficiency of the judge's charge,618 or to the form of the indictment,619 or to the jurisdiction of the court,620 or to any There having been no abuse of judicial discretion in denying the motion for a new trial, there was no ruling of law to which the petitioner could have saved a valid exception if he had received notice of the action of the court, and he therefore was not prejudiced by not receiving such a notice."

Granting or refusal of a motion to set aside a verdict and to grant a new trial on the ground of newly discovered evidence "ordinarily rests in the sound judicial discretion of the trial judge, whose function is to decide whether that which is alleged to be newly discovered evidence is in truth of that nature, whether it is credible in character, whether it relates to vital aspects of the case, whether it is merely cumulative, and whether on a survey of the whole case a miscarriage of justice will result if a new trial is not granted; such considerations are likely to be more accurately weighed and a wise and just decision rendered by the magistrate who presided throughout the trial than by any one else." 622 The general law has been thus

Rugg, C. J., of the controlling principles of law respecting the granting of motions for new trial on the ground of newly discovered evidence. The determination of a motion for a new trial of an action at law on the ground of newly discovered evidence rests within the sound judicial discretion of the trial judge. Davis v. Boston Elevated, 

235 Mass. 482. To same effect, Com-

summed up by the court:-"Doubtless new trials are not to be granted on the ground of newly discovered evidence except upon proof of important evidence of such a nature as to be likely to have a material effect upon the result, which could not reasonably have been discovered before the trial by the exercise of proper diligence and respecting the production of which on motion there has been an entire want of laches. A new trial ordinarily will not be granted upon the discovery of evidence which is cumulative and in most such cases will and ought to be denied." 628 "The mischief naturally flowing from retrials based upon the discovery of alleged new evidence leads to the establishment of a somewhat stringent practice against granting such motions unless upon a survey of the whole case a miscarriage of justice is likely to result if a new trial is denied. This is the fundamental test, in aid of which most if not all the rules upon the matter from time to time alluded to, have been formulated. 

Ease in obtaining new trials would offer temptations to the securing of fresh evidence to supply former deficiencies. But courts cannot close 'their eyes to injustice on account of facility of abuse.' Nevertheless, most critical scrutiny must be given to the kind of evidence offered in support of the motion, to the sources from which it comes, and the circumstances under which it is produced." 624 Simply because newly discovered evidence is material and admissible, the party in whose favor it is, is not entitled as of right to a new trial; 625—but in such case a new monwealth v. At the trial of an action of tort for malicious prosecution and false arrest, the plaintiff and his daughter testified that the plaintiff was arrested on a warrant, procured by the defendant, and was handcuffed and, while so handcuffed and on the way to the police station, met acquaintances. The defendant moved for a new trial, supporting his motion by affidavits of three police officers, that no handcuffs were used upon the plaintiff and that no one was met on the journey to the station except a police officer. There was no evidence that the juror was addicted to the use of intoxicants or of drugs, and there was not evidence that his faculties were beclouded or that he was under the influence of intoxicating liquor or drugs at any time when he was sitting as a member of the jury it cannot be said with truth that the juror was disqualified for a proper deliberation and exercise of his reason and judgment; however much such conduct is justly open to severe criticism and stinging reproof, the exception to the refusal to grant a new trial because of the alleged drunkenness of the juror must be overruled. Declaring a mistrial. If the court believes that a trial for any reason is proceeding in a materially unfair manner he may on his own motion discharge the jury. The rule has been thus stated. "The court if it believes that unproven matters which occur in the conduct of a trial will result in a false verdict, may declare a mistrial." 699 Hence, when remarks of counsel bring a false issue before the jury and tend to bring about a mistrial, the court may withdraw the case from the jury. The trial court who is in the atmosphere of the trial is the best judge of the effect of these irrelevant statements of counsel which tend to prejudice.700 The court has thus summarized a situation. "If the judge, acting impartially, as we must assume he did, believed that the statement of counsel was likely to result in an unjust verdict, we cannot say that his action was without justification. Of course, he could not exercise the power vested in him to act arbitrarily, or without good cause to believe that the action he took was necessary to prevent great injustice either to the Commonwealth or to the defendant. d. Framing issues for jury: Submitting questions: Report. 

Whenever the decision of a civil case depends on a principle of law and that principle is not so clearly established that the trial court can instruct the jury accurately and positively as to its effect as applied to the case on trial, the judge "shall by appropriate questions to the jury, or by his own findings when the trial is without a jury, ascertain as far as is practicable all the facts both as to liability and damages, necessary on any theory of the law to enable the court to make the proper final disposition of the case, unless in the opinion of the court such a course is inexpedient under the circumstances of the case. When special questions are submitted to a jury, the judge may or may not take a general verdict and may report the case on the answers of the jury, or make such other order therein as he deems proper. A court reporting to the full court for its determination a question as to the correctness of any ruling of law made by him at a trial or on a motion for a new trial, may make in any proper case a provision in the report that, if his rulings were correct, a judgment or decree shall be entered for the party in whose favor the ruling was made, and that, if his rulings were wrong, the judgment or decree shall be entered in accordance with such rulings as he ought to have made." 708 In civil cases in the Supreme Judicial Court a single justice in his discretion may report a case to the full bench.704 In the superior court on

111 the aim of consolidation.790 The court may order cases pending in the same county which involve the same issues and parties to be tried together or separately.791 The mere fact that such trial will admit against one party evidence not admissible against another will not require that no joint trial be had.792 

The court in such trials by proper instructions on request must protect the rights of the parties.798 In considering consolidation and joint trials three classes of cases and methods of procedure are to be noted. First; where several cases are pending on different causes of action involving in substance but one question, a court has "inherent power to prevent the scandal to the administration of justice which would result from a trial of each case separately and as one method of avoiding it may stay proceedings in all cases but one and see whether the disposition of that one may not settle the others." 794 This course established elsewhere,795 in Massachusetts is not common. Second; "where several causes are pending between the same or different parties which grow out of a single transaction or which involve an inquiry into the same event in its general aspects, although the details of evidence may vary materially in fixing responsibility, the court may order them tried together. But they continue separate so far as they concern docket entries, verdicts, judgments, and all aspects save only the one of joint trial. This is a frequent practice and finds many illustrations in our decisions." 796 It is to a consolidation of this kind that reference was made by Mr. Justice Gray in Mutual Life Ins. Co. v. Hillman, 145 U. S. 285, in saying at p. 293, "But although the defendants might lawfully be compelled, at the discretion of the

Each record is that of an independent suit, except in so far as the evidence in one is, by order of the court, treated as evidence in both. The consolidation does not change the rules of equity pleading, nor the rights of the parties, as those rights must still turn on the pleadings, proofs, and proceedings in their respective suits. The parties in one suit do not thereby become parties in the other, and a decree in one is not a decree in the other, unless so directed." 797 Third: "When several cases are pending which might have been made the subject of a single suit or action, the court may enter an order which shall fuse the several proceedings into a single one. The original actions lose their identity and become merged into the one in which alone the rights of the parties will be determined. Thereafter they are conducted not as separate and distinct actions or suits, but as one. In suits in equity, where there are several different parties but the same res is the subject of the litigation, or where there is such identity in the nature of the proceeding, the interests of the parties, or the relief to be afforded, as to require or render highly expedient a unification of divers proceedings, an order of consolidation in appropriate instances may bring all into one suit." 798

OPINION 

Present Stone, J. The question presented by this report is the right of a defendant to a trial by jury in a case wherein the plaintiff seeks to substitute a new declaration for his original declaration. 

The plaintiff began his action by a writ dated January 3, 1925. By so doing the plaintiff waived his right to a trial by jury.

General Laws, Chapter 231, Section 

103. 

Acts 1922, Chapter 532, Section 8. 

The defendant had a right within two days after filing his appearance to claim a trial by jury and have the case removed to the Superior Court. 

Failing to do so he must be held to have waived this right. Such a statute which compels a party to claim his trial by jury or else be held to waive it is constitutional. 

Hapgood vs. Doherty, 8 Gray 373. 

Foster v. Morse, 132 Mass. 354.

While the Legislature does not have the power to deprive a party of this right it has, according to the acts last cited, the power 'to make all manner of wholesome and reasonable orders, laws, statutes and ordinances, directions or instructions regulating the mode in which this right shall be enjoyed or used.' We do not understand that the defendant controverts this principle. 

It appeared, however, that some time after the defendant had waived in this way his right to trial by jury and approximately at the time of the trial of the case the plaintiff desired to amend his declaration. This amendment in brief substituted for a declaration on an account annexed for goods, a declaration upon a promissory note.

The defendant objected to the allowance of this amendment but it was allowed by the court. We do not understand the defendant as denying the right of the judge at his discretion to allow the pleadings to be amended in this way. 

What the defendant does say, however, is that the allowance of this amendment substitutes one kind of a cause of action for another substantially different and practically is allowing the plaintiff to start a new 'controversy' and that because the court has allowed that to be done the defendant is, as a matter of right, en-

THE COURT 

117 and rule of court, it cannot be claimed as of right. The court's titled to claim trial by jury at the time when the amendment is allowed. 

In order to bring this matter to the court the defendant filed two motions, one to transfer the case to the Superior Court for trial by jury and another to be permitted to file the necessary papers for removal to the Superior Court as if the same had been filed within the time prescribed by the statute. The court denied both these motions in its discretion and reported the case to the Appellate Division with the stipulation that if the defendant was entitled to the allowance of these motions or either of them the case was to be removed to the Superior Court otherwise such order is to be made as is proper in the premises.

There is some ground for holding that this is not a proper subject for report. 

The duty of removing a case to the Superior Court is not placed upon the court but upon the Clerk. It is a matter of administration rather than judi- Icial decision. Under certain circumstances a party is entitled as of right to have his case removed to the Superior Court. If the Clerk of the court did not act it is perhaps doubtful whether the judge of the Court should order him to do so. Possibly the proper remedy would be by an application to the Supreme Judicial Court for a writ of mandamus. We mention this but prefer to decide the case upon its merits as reported. Even if mandamus would lie in such a case it may not be the only remedy. As a general rule the judges of the court are clothed with power to instruct their Clerks to obey statute requirements. If we are to decide this question the motions filed by the defendant would either of them seem to raise the question which he desires adjudicated. We have, therefore, to consider whether the defendant's constitutional right to a trial by jury has been invaded by the action of the court. If it has, then the allowance of the motions was not within the discretion of the court but was a matter of right. Otherwise unless the exercise of discretion can be said as a matter of law to be unreasonable the parties and this tribunal are bound by the decision of the single justice. 

In so far as the decision of this question depends upon the constitutionality of the statute above cited, this court need only consider the question as to whether the Supreme Judicial Court has ever declared that the statute violates any provision of the Constitution. Until such an adjudication has been made by that court the strong presumption of constitutionality which attaches to all acts of the supreme legislative body constrains us to decide against the defendant on that branch of the case. It does not appear that the Supreme Judicial Court has ever declared this statute unconstitutional. 

On the contrary the statute has been assumed to be constitutional by that court. 

Commonwealth v. Leach, 246 Mass. 464, 473. 

If this statute is constitutional, it seems that the parties have no right to claim an appeal so as to obtain trial by jury unless they comply with the statute. Confessedly the defendant has not made his election in time. He did not 'within two days after the time allowed for entering his appearance file in said court a claim of trial by jury.' 

The defendant points out, however, that the district court 'may upon cause shown and after notice to all adverse parties permit such removal to the Superior Court upon the terms above specified at any time prior to final judgment.'

General Laws, Chapter 231, Section 

107. 

Acts 1922, Chapter 532, Section 8. 

The defendant further says that in order to secure to him his right of trial by jury it was the duty of the judge acting under the section just quoted to order the case transferred to the Superior Court and that in such a case as is here presented the word 'may' is the equivalent of 'shall.' 

This contention does not seem to be warranted. In the first place, it is to be doubted if the Legislature intended that this permission to remove to the

discretion then prevails. If a motion to amend is denied, the 

Superior Court should be used as a means of avoiding the express wording of the statute. If it had been the intention of the Legislature that under certain circumstances the appeal to the Superior Court could be entered after the two days had expired it would have been comparatively simple to have granted to the court the privilege of extending the time for cause shown. 

This was not done and it seems, therefore, that the Legislature in the section referred to merely intended to give the district courts power to transfer to the Superior Court any case in which it seemed to them a trial by jury was desirable. If this is the interpretation of the statute it is obvious that such action of the court is a matter of discretion and not of absolute right.

This seems to be borne out by the decisions in this Commonwealth. While this precise question has not been before the Supreme Judicial Court a question strikingly similar has been adjudicated by that court on many occasions. 

In 1852 the Legislature prescribed that in order to obtain a trial by jury the party desiring such a trial must Iclaim it within a certain time or else be held to have waived that right.

Acts of 1852, Chapter 314. 

This provision of the law exists at the present time. 60. 

General Laws, Chapter 231, Section 

The similarity in the situation created by this statute and the one with regard to the district courts is obvious. Under this statute it has been held that one who does not claim a trial by jury within the time specified takes the risk of subsequent amendments allowed by the courts which materially change the aspect of the case: 'If the party does not file a notice that he desires a trial by jury he takes the risk of any amendment that may thereafter be allowed by the court, and after the time provided for filing such a notice has elapsed it is in the discretion of the court on amendments being allowed which change the issues or introduce new issues to grant or deny to any party the right to file the notice required by the statute.' 

Cleverly v. O'Connell, 156 Mass. 88. 

See also, Bailey v. Joy, 132 Mass. 356. 

Clark v. Baker, 192 Mass. 226.

These decisions seem to us to be decisive of the case at bar. That the words of the court in deciding 

Cleverly v. O'Connell, 156 Mass. 88 (cited supra) were carefully considered is shown by the fact that in many cases in which absolutely new issues are involved which the parties did not and probably could not have known at the time the action was started the Supreme Judicial Court has held that the matter of allowing a trial by jury was nevertheless a matter of discretion. 

In a suit on a bond in which a jury trial was not claimed, after the court has decided as to the validity of the bond the defendant desired a trial by jury as to the matter of damages but it was held that it was within the discretion of the court to deny this claim. 

Vitrified Wheel and Emery Co. v. 

Edwards, 135 Mass. 591.

In a case on a mechanic's lien where trial by jury was not claimed and the court admitted a new party as a defendant it was held that the plaintiff was not entitled as a matter of right to trial by jury. 

Graham v. Lord, 170 Mass. 1.

See also in a scire facias on a bond where the defendant filed an amended answer which presented a different issue from the one originally before the court it was held that it was in the discretion of the trial court to refuse to allow one of the parties to claim trial by jury. In this case it should be noted, however, that the waiver of trial by jury was in writing and signed by the parties. The principle, however, is the same. 

Thompson v. King, 173 Mass. 439.

Perhaps the most striking illustration of this principle is found in cases under the Workmen's Compensation Act. By this statute an employee is held to have waived his right to an action at common law unless he notifies his employer

A court by amendment may correct errors in its judgments 838 but after a verdict is recorded in the absence of statute the court cannot amend the verdict.889 Though a judgment partly satisfied cannot be vacated,840 yet an "execution upon a judgment partially satisfied although it erroneously states the amount of the judgment is amendable and is voidable only and any action under it is valid even if it is not amended." 841 The court will correct technical errors in its papers. 842 In making amendments, courts, if the facts warrant, may allow amendments nunc pro tunc.848 In allowing amendments there is a limit on the court's that he does not intend to accept the provisions of the statute. If he does not, in a suit at common law his damages are assessed by the Industrial Accident Board on an entirely different principle than the one he might submit to a jury. It is obvious that at the time an employee takes up his employment the cause of any action due to the negligence of his employer cannot be held to have arisen and yet it has been decided that by making his election at this time he necessarily waives his right to trial by jury on the question of damages which he sustained. 

In other words, the 'controversy' to use the words of the Declaration of Rights has not yet arisen. The action of the citizen in question is held to be a waiver of his constitutional right to trial by jury.

It is true that the questions of whether the employer has brought himself within the terms of the act and the question of whether the employee did give notice or not may still be decided by a jury if the employee brings an act at common law but if those facts are decided against him the important questions of the merits of his controversy are to be determined by an administrative board and his constitutional right to have them determined by a jury of his peers is held to have been waived. 

Young v. Duncan, 218 Mass. 346.

It seems, therefore, that in the case at bar the motions intended to secure a trial by jury were addressed to the discretion of the court and as that discretion does not seem as a matter of law to have been unreasonably exercised it follows that they were properly denied.

The order should be made therefore 'report dismissed' and the case should be returned to the district court of

In а divorce proceeding a decree granting a divorce placed the children in the custody of the mother, the libellant, and ordered the libellee to pay a certain sum for their support and to pay for medical services to be rendered by a certain physician. That physician died and thereafter the libellant employed a specialist for one of the children. Subsequently she filed a motion for a modification of the decree which was heard by a judge who filed a memorandum of findings and a suggestion for a decree directing an increase of the amount which the libellee should pay for the support and maintenance of the children and that the selection of physicians for the children should be left to the libellant. More than four years and nine months thereafter and nearly eleven months after a decision by this court, in an action at law by the specialist against the libellee for his services, in the face of a claimed defense to the effect that the libellee was not liable because the divorce decree did not authorize the libellant to employ the specialist and the libellee had not assented thereto, the judge indorsed upon a draft of a decree, which had been drawn in accordance with suggestions in his memorandum excepting that it omitted the direction that the selection of physicians should be left to the libellant, an order allowing the decree and directing that it take effect as of the date of the memorandum, and also a further order, to take effect as of a date previous to the date when the services were rendered by the specialist, that the original decree be modified to allow the libellant to make the selection of proper medical attendance for the children. Held, that it was within the power of the court to cause such decree to be entered nunc pro tunc, and, both parties being before the court, that they were concluded by it so far as their rights as to one another were concerned. It also was held that the order thus entered nunc pro tunc in the divorce proceedings had no effect to establish liability on the part of the libellee for the services of the specialist selected and employed by the libellant when she had no authority to do so.

When justice requires the court, even after both parties have rested and the charge has been com- 36 872 The exception to the denial of the defendant's motion to require the plaintiff to elect whether to proceed on counts one and two based upon a rescission, or upon count three based upon a breach of warranty, must be overruled. The fact that the plaintiff in certain counts seeks to recover on the ground of rescission does not as matter of law preclude it from establishing liability on another ground in case its attempted rescission should be held to be ineffectual. It is in the interests of accomplishing justice in a case of this kind to have all material issues of fact decided, so that the case may be finally determined in one trial if it should appear as matter of law that the action cannot be maintained on any of the counts or that it may be maintained on certain counts and not in others.

In determining whether this material evidence, or the evidence which constituted the foundation, shall be first presented the court's discretion will not be disturbed.881 The subject of the court's discretion in receiving evidence divides into four logical divisions, the first pertaining to the qualifications of the witness, the second pertaining to the nature of the evidence and number of witnesses, the third pertaining to the order of its presentation and the fourth pertaining to the form of examination of the witness. These in so far as they pertain to discretion 882 are considered in their order. 

(2) Qualification of witnesses-(a) Generally. The subject of the qualifications of a witness is later considered.888 Here we consider only the discretion of the court as it pertains to that subject. Whether a witness is qualified is partly a preliminary question of fact; 884 but after hearing the facts and determining what is the true status, whether the witness should be sworn lies largely in the court's discretion.885 Here are four questions that may arise,-first, is the witness physically able to attend; second, is he mentally capable to observe and to testify; 887 third, is he qualified to testify as to the matters in regard to which he is offered as an expert,888 and fourth, is he totally disqualified.889

"Competency: A recent case in Con necticut is worthy of note. In a suit for seduction, the trial court was held to have exceeded his discretion in permitting a feeble minded girl of fifteen years to testify. The witness testified that she did not know the difference between right and wrong, had never heard of a Supreme Being, did not know what the word God meant, had never heard of the hereafter, and did not know what the obligation of an oath was and what would happen if she did not tell the truth except that she would be in trouble. She testified that she knew what an oath was because she could see it in court. She did not realize what the defendant was doing at the time of the intercourse and did not know for a considerable time of her pregnancy. Experts testified that she was not mentally deranged, could read and write a simple letter and make simple arithmetical computations, that she was definitely defective in judgment and comprehension. At the time of the trial she was an inmate of the 

State School for the Feeble Minded. 

She should not have been permitted to testify and to establish such accusations on her unsupported testimony.

"'899 (3) Nature of the evidence and number of witnesses-(a) Generally. The nature of the evidence offered determines the right of the court in its discretion to exclude or admit it. A clear oral express admission if not remote in time must be admitted. On the other hand events which might be construed as an admission of guilt, if they occurred long after the event may be excluded as remote.900 So in many of the classes of evidence that are admissible under the "exceptions to the rules of exclusion," attendant circumstances may render evidence admissible or inadmissible.901 Many factors frequently are to be balanced and unless discretion is abused the final admission or exclusion of the evidence will not be disturbed. Certain evidence though of some probative value is so uncertain and so likely to be prejudicial that the court even in its discretion cannot admit it. This is under a rule which will be set out in Part II. An illustration is the evidence, so frequently offered, of the acts and mental sensations of spectators at or near the scene of a collision. Evidence that a bystander was "concerned" or "frightened" by the speed of a car is said to have no probative value to show excessive speed.910 "Expletive superlatives" such as statements that a car was going "terribly fast" or "awful fast" or "very fast" do not show an excessive negligent speed.911 Yet the court has referred to such evidence as of some probative value.912 The court seems to hold that evidence of a bystander's fright when offered to show that the speed of a vehicle was excessive, is immaterial.918 So evidence

THE COURT 

129 that a party is insured against accident is not admissible to show that he, therefore, was less regardful of his liability and accordingly negligent.914 The exclusion of such matters though based on the proposition that the evidence would mislead the jury or create a prejudice is required by law; it is not a matter of discretion. Hence, the rule that excludes evidence which is likely to mislead or prejudice the jury is one of wide range and of varying degrees of intensity. At one extreme evidence which would have this effect is excluded absolutely, at the other extreme the evidence must be admitted if within any principle of law which makes it unquestionably competent. Between these two extremes lies an undescribable field of discretion. The point at which exclusion ends and discretion begins is not to be located in any set rule. As probative evidence approaches the point where law requires its exclusion, the field of discretion begins.915 

The point where exclusion is required as a matter of law is treated later.916 (c) Best evidence: Inaccurate documents. A court formerly had discretion in requiring that all proof be made by the "best. evidence." The principle has been thus expressed. "Where it is incumbent on a plaintiff to prove a fact and he refuses to prove it by the best evidence which is open to him all other evidence may properly be excluded and the plaintiff's case will fail for lack of evidence." 917 In all matters but those which pertain to writings, or real evidence, or exhibits, this rule seems either obsolete or obsolescent.918 The "best evidence rule" as applied to writings and real evidence or exhibits and the field of discretion therein is considered in Part V.919 A court in its discretion may exclude a document which it finds inaccurate.920 excluded the question, subject to the plaintiff's exception; there was nothing to show what answer was expected from the witness. 940 Hunt v. Lowell Gas Light Co., 8 

Allen 169. Two cases should be contrasted; both are suits in tort for injury caused from escaping gas. The circumstances and results are set out in the following words from the decisions. In the first "The evi- dence offered by the plaintiffs to show that wherever the gas which escaped from the fracture in the defendants' pipe entered any dwelling house in the neighborhood of the plaintiffs, sickness followed, was properly excluded. Each separate and individual case must stand upon, and be decided by the evidence particularly applicable to it. The attending circumstances may be so different, that the occurrence of sickness in one house would have no tendency to show the cause of illness in the occupants of another.'' If such evidence was admissible, the "issues in a single cause might be indefinitely multiplied; and this would tend only to confusion, and to mislead the jury.' "It was competent for the plaintiffs to show all the facts and circumstances attending their sickness, and to add to that, proof of the opinions of persons of skill 

and experience as to the cause which produced such sickness, and particularly whether it might have been, or probably was, produced by the gas to which they were exposed in their house; but they were restricted by the rules of evidence to these limits, and could not establish or strengthen the evidence in their own case, by any proof concerning the condition of, or the injuries received by, another person.

Emerson v. Lowell Gas Light Co., 3 

Allen 410. In the second, "The plaintiffs were visitors in the family of Aaron Hunt at the time when the defendants' gas escaped into the house, and they were permitted to offer evidence that Aaron Hunt and his family had been in perfect health up to the time when the gas began to escape into their house, and that, immediately or soon after, every member of the family became seriously sick. The admission of this evidence is excepted to. But evidence of this character was held to be admissible in the case of Aaron Hunt against these defendants. 1 Allen 344.

The plaintiffs were not allowed to give evidence of the particulars of the sickness of any one of these persons; and it is objected that, if the evidence was admissible to any extent, the particulars should have been inquired into. But the sickness of these persons is a collateral fact, and is admissible merely for the purpose of showing the nature of the gas which came into the house, to the influence of which all the inmates were subjected alike. (4) Order of evidence: Time of ruling on admissibility—(a) 

Introductory. The term "order of evidence" as used in the decisions has two meanings;-the order in which the parties proceed in the presentation of their side of the case, and the order in which the facts offered by one party to prove a proposition are presented. The order of evidence in the first sense is usually for the plaintiff to present his case, for the defendant to follow with presentation of his facts or contradiction of the plaintiff's, for the plaintiff to present his rebuttal to these facts presented by the defendant and for the defendant to follow in rebuttal of the plaintiff's rebuttal; the court, however, in its discretion to some extent may change this order. The order of evidence in the second sense is wholly in the court's discretion. (b) Rebuttal anticipated in plaintiff's presentation. The plaintiff usually presents his facts first. He is to make out the issues as set by the declaration. If he anticipates the defense and presents in his direct case matters of rebuttal he may thereby lose his right to present the same facts or matters in rebuttal.949 He also may lose his right to rely solely on the issues raised by his declaration and the defendant's answer. 959 De Bene.-Caution should be used in admitting; prejudice where evidence finally stricken out. The trial lasted eight days. Once or twice during the trial the plaintiff offered evidence which was received by the judge "de bene.”

Later it was stricken out and the jury instructed wholly to disregard it. No legal ground of exception here is disclosed. (Citing, Whitney v. Bayley, 4

Allen 173.) It is assumed that in this ruling "de bene" was used not in the technical sense in which it occurs sometimes in statutes (see 6 Encyc. Pleading & Practice, 625) but as meaning conditionally or provisionally upon its connection with the matters on trial being later shown, or upon its competency or relevancy being made to appear at a subsequent stage. In a long trial of complicated issues, much must be left in this regard to the discretion of the presiding judge. Nevertheless, great caution ought to be exercised as the trial goes forward that evidence which can have at best only a remote bearing upon the points in controversy, should not be admitted. The danger of an unconscious influence from evidence once received, although subsequently stricken out, is pointed out forceably by Mr. Justice Hammond, in Newman v. Newman, 211 Mass. 509. But it does not appear that there was any abuse of discretion or that anything was done which requires the sustaining of this exception. (Citing, Commonwealth 

Johnson, 199 Mass. 55, 59.) Clarke v. 

City of Fall River, 219 Mass. 580.

THE COURT 

139 (f) Evidence admitted "de bene." The term "de bene" 960 has several meanings.961 It is in other jurisdictions used in connection with the certification of depositions.962 In Massachusetts when evidence is admitted "de bene" that term in the sense here employed means in substance that the evidence seems to the court to have sufficient probable connection with the case to permit its admission with the understanding that if its immateriality finally becomes evident, the court on motion shall order it stricken out.963 When there is a chain of facts of which every link is necessary to show relevancy of the main fact or of any of the facts, the court may admit any link on the assumption that the whole shall be presented.964 Each link as offered should be objected to; and the fact that the evidence is received "de bene" should appear on the record. If the materiality of the evidence later appears, it stands. If it does not,-if the connecting links of the chain do not appear,-on motion the evidence admitted "de bene," if immaterial at the time of passing on the motion to strike out, must be stricken out.965 If no motion

At the trial of an action of tort for deceit by a woman against one who was the president and treasurer of a corporation owning real estate, the plaintiff contended that the defendant falsely represented that he was authorized by the corporation to employ her as a broker to procure a purchaser of some of its real estate, that she procured a customer and that the directors of the corporation refused to effectuate the sale. It appeared that the plaintiff had brought an action against the corporation for her commission at the trial of which a verdict was ordered for the corporation. The plaintiff was allowed de bene to introduce evidence tending to show that the counsel for the corporation in seeking the ordering of that verdict had contended that the stockholders of the corporation had not authorized the directors to sell the real estate. The evidence was stricken out and the plaintiff excepted. The jury found for the defendant. Held, that the evidence properly was stricken out, the defendant as an individual not being a party to that action and the statements by the corporation's counsel not being admissions by him. The state of the issues at the time of the offer of evidence may effect the admissibility.984 If evidence is admissible under the issues as they stand at the time when the evidence is offered and it is admitted, though the particular issue on which it is admitted later may be withdrawn, no exception to its admission will be sustained.985 If the opponent wishes it stricken out, he must move to strike it out.986 If such evidence is erroneously excluded, if the issue on which it is admissible is withdrawn, there is no injury to the objecting party and hence no exception based on its exclusion will be sustained. 984 The defendants had contended that they were justified in removing the plaintiff from office because he had left large sums of the city's money on deposit with a certain bank in preference to other banks and had failed to collect sums due to the city from that bank as interest on daily balances. It also appeared that actions at law had been brought against the plaintiff and the sureties on his official bond, after his removal from the office to which he later was reinstated, for failure to collect such interest. Subject to exceptions by the defendants, the plaintiff was allowed to testify that he had had a conversation with one of the defendants in which that defendant had stated that he would "get even" with the president of the bank in question because its president had refused to honor his note, and also to testify that he had been informed from various sources that there was no ground for the action against him and the sureties on his bond. Held, that the testimony as to the conversation with one of the defendants was admissible as tending to show malice toward the plaintiff, (which then was an issue, although it later was withdrawn as an issue by the plaintiff,) and that both that conversation and the other testimony of the plaintiff were admissible as tending to refute the defendants' contention that the plaintiff's mental suffering was caused, not by their wrongful action in removing him, but by the controversy as to the relations between the plaintiff and the bank in question. S. To maintain the dignity of the court: Parties' agreements to arbitrate: Contempt. The court has the duty to maintain the dignity of the law. In this respect it must not without statute 1090 permit parties to oust the court of jurisdiction or to set up a tribunal of their own as a substitute for the court; 1081 and it, if its dignity is infringed upon, has full power of prosecuting for contempt.1032

I. Matters applicable to jury and to other arbiters of fact, p. 254. 

I. Introductory. An important, if not the chief, feature of the system which involves trial by jury, is the separation of the functionary of the tribunal which determines the law, and the functionary which determines the facts. The human race before trial by jury has known many methods of settling disputes between parties;-by the employment of force, by the casting of lot, by invoking divine guidance, by trial by battle or by water, by secret investigations and inquisition, by reference to arbitrators and by many other methods. In these methods of "trial," there usually was no separation of law and fact; the whole case was determined by a judgment which to the judge

or supervising body unhampered by precedent, seemed adequate or just. No rule of law governed the method of finding of facts. 

In stating fixed rules of law Moses, Solon and Draco were pioneers. The separation of principles of law and matters of fact was the first step in permanent legal progress. When rules of law were once established and interpreted, the chief duty of a magistrate was to determine facts. In a country which is not progressive, in a staple simple community where few new questions arise,-administration of law becomes simple, lawyers may be few, judges need but read summaries of former decisions, and the disposal of cases is without complication. Once set the law and the determination of the facts is quick and usually accurate. Few jurists have become famous because they have found from conflicting facts the truth. In a progressive nation, there is a complication of laws. New questions, almost hourly, arise. Legislatures, bureaus and even executives are issuing acts, rules or proclamations which have the force of law. In doing so frequently they exceed their constitutional authority. 

Rules and statutes may conflict. To know the law, even reasonably well, one must devote much time to its study. Administration of justice becomes complicated and requires judges who shall not be overburdened with the duty of determining facts. One whose life is given to following the learned minds which have formulated and are formulating law may lose much of the "common touch." Such person is not so well prepared to pass on the credibility of a witness or party as the man drawn from every day life, to serve on a jury. Hence in such community the jury system stands as the most accurate method of ascertaining from conflicting facts the truth. 

II. Systems of determining facts-A. Introductory. The jury system in so far as it separates law and fact has been adequate; and in trials of great importance is clearly the most trusted and most reliable procedure. Experiment tends to tolerate other systems. We now have boards which specialize in certain classes of cases, rule on the law, find the facts, and subject to the court's approval decide cases within their special province.¹ We also have administrative bodies which in the course of their administration hear matters of fact. We have

arbitrators, auditors, masters," referees, commissioners," and judges & trying law and fact. Their procedure and powers vary with the statutes or customs which create them. 

B. Boards specializing on certain subjects: Finding of fact: 

Rules of evidence. When a board, in part administrative and in part judicial, is created by statute, to regulate the administration of the laws applicable to a certain branch of the law and to decide cases arising thereunder, whether the rules of evidence shall apply depends on the importance of the judicial functions of that board. If it sits as a court, it usually observes the rules of evidence. Frequently the rulings of such board on questions of law may be passed on by the Courts; its findings of fact usually are final. Illustrations of such boards are the Industrial 

Accident Board and the Interstate Commerce Commission. 

C.

Administrative boards making investigations as a part of administrative duties: School committees: City councils and like bodies. When an "administrative board clothed with quasi judicial powers" is called on to consider matters of fact presented at an authorized and required hearing, if it appears that the members of the board are impartial,10 that a fair trial has been given, and that the party claiming unfairness has been allowed to present the merits of his cause, mere errors committed in the admission or exclusion of evidence are not enough to make invalid a final adverse decision.11 Good faith on the part of such board is a requisite 12 of a fair hearing; but when there is good faith and a reasonable opportunity to present his case given each party, the findings of fact made by such board unless clearly wrong will not be disturbed.18 Within this class

D. Arbitration-1. Generally. Arbitration is a frequent method for settling disputes and determining facts. Arbitrators usually do not draw a sharp distinction between law and fact. 

They attempt to settle disputes fairly by direct methods.15 

Three classes of arbitration are to be distinguished, those not approved by statute but created by parties, whose award is not a condition precedent to suit,-those not approved by statute, but created by parties, whose award is a condition precedent to suit and those existing by the parties' consent and approved by statute. These are now considered. 

2. Nonstatutory arbitration created by parties, award not a condition precedent of suit. Parties cannot by agreement, in the absence of statute, oust the courts of jurisdiction;16 hence an executory agreement not authorized by statute that they shall submit any future dispute to arbitration for final decision is voidable." If, however, the parties act on such mutual agreement and a conclusion is reached by the arbitrators, the person who has submitted to the jurisdiction of the arbitrators in the absence of fraud or unfairness will not be heard to complain that the result was unjust.18 Agreements which assist courts and shorten trials are to be distinguished. So parties without statute may agree that damages shall be set by arbitrators and such agreement is probably enforceable.19 In such hearings, the rules of evidence, if the arbitrators, not unlimited by terms of the agreement, so elect, do not apply.20 The findings of facts by the arbitrators in matters fully heard with the co-operation of all parties, in the absence of fraud or like matter and in the absence of agreement to the contrary or statute, usually are final.21

The decision of arbitrators if made in good faith will be prima facie,52 or conclusive,58 according to the reference and report of the referees 54 or agreement of the parties, or the terms of the statute.56 Method of procedure when not expressly established by the statute or by the agreement for arbitrating lies within the discretion of the board of arbitrators.57 The strict rules of evidence need not be followed,58 and in some cases no notice of meetings need be given the parties and no open hearings need be had.59 Probably 55

At common law, as said above, courts would not specifically enforce agreements to arbitrate.78 Part performance of a contract which calls for arbitration however may affect the court's attitude."79 If an arbitration has been unfair,80 or the arbitrators prejudiced, if the objecting party is not estopped to claim the unfairness or prejudice, the award on proper action may be set aside.81 A party, however, who knowingly accepts arbitrators who have displayed prejudice, and proceeds with a hearing without objection to its conclusion and to the award may be estopped to set up the arbitrators' disqualification.82 It seems against natural rights that an arbitrator should be a party to the dispute which he is to decide.88 This is particularly so if the party acting as arbitrator shows a dishonest attitude, or renders the arbitration impossible; 85 by so doing he may render arbitration, even if a condition precedent to suit, unnecessary.

2. Auditor-a. Introductory. Auditors may be appointed in actions at law, in matters in the probate court and probably in divorce proceedings. In all of these proceedings the rules of evidence govern. In an action at law procedure before auditors is well established. In probate proceedings the procedure differs.104 

We consider the more important matters pertaining to the finding of fact before auditors in matters at law. b. Appointment of auditors. In all courts a legal action may be referred to an auditor.105 In all courts but the lower courts the reference rests wholly within the court's discretion. In the lower courts the consent of all parties is necessary before a case may be ruled to an auditor.106 An auditor formerly was an officer who considered cases wherein accounts were involved, but any type of case now may be referred to him. His findings of fact are but prima facie evidence unless by the rule they are made final. 107 C.

Powers under the rule (1) Fact. Usually an auditor finds only fact and his findings as shown by his report are but prima facie evidence to be used at the trial. By agreement of the parties and by order of the court his findings of fact may be final.108 His report is then treated as the report of a referee 109 and his findings of fact are final.110 His report in such case should not review the evidence and discuss the law and fact of the case, but should set forth his conclusions of fact.111 (2) Law (a) Apart from rulings on evidence. An auditor is not to pass on the law.112 If in his findings he sets out rulings

Method of raising questions of errors in admitting or excluding evidence. In hearings before auditors if a party objects to the admission or exclusion of evidence and the auditor overrules his objection admitting or excluding the evidence the objection should be noted and the question duly reserved for the later ruling of the trial court.128 The offers of proof and form of objection should be as in trials in open court.124 The auditor should be requested to set out in his report all material facts and rulings which pertain to his decision on the admission or exclusion of evidence.125 When the report is filed if the questions raised at the hearing and all matters connected therewith are not fairly presented the objecting party should move to recommit; and on hearing on such motion when he seeks to correct errors in the admission or exclusion of evidence, again he may present his objections to the alleged erroneous ruling.126

3. Masters-a. Introductory. Masters under various forms of appointments and with various duties are frequently named in suits in equity. A master's report stands differently from an auditor's.218 His findings of fact properly found are usually final.219 Though when all the facts from which a master draws conclusions are in his report, the court may draw conclusions at variance with his, yet the usual rule is that a master's findings of fact will not be disturbed.220 b. Appointment. The appointments of masters set their duties.221 The forms of reference most common, indicate that the nature of their reports and the contents will vary. If the reference directs the master to hear the parties and their evidence, to find the facts and to report the same to the court, the master is not required to set out the testimony or to summarize it; he simply reports the facts and his findings thereon to the court.328 If the reference requires the master to report such findings of auditor on same evidence and such other evidence as parties might introduce should be final, on motion to recommit case to auditor, evidence and affidavits as to testimony and evidence at previous trials were not competent. On exceptions after judgment on report of auditor, Supreme 

Judicial Court will not consider evidentiary matters, and review or revise findings of fact. On exceptions after judgment entered on findings of audi tor from evidence, Supreme Judicial 

Court will not consider matters depending on testimony and evidence, and review or revise findings of fact.- 

Finding of auditor is final on mere statement of fact. On a mere statement of fact, finding of auditor to whom case has been referred to consider evidence and make findings of fact is final.

309 The following is the charge of

Judge Williams with a portion of the report of the case in the Boston Herald of May 14, 1929: "Rumors persisted yesterday that the grand jurors were all ready to summon Chairman Dowling of the finance commission and Judge 

Sullivan of the school survey committee.

Whatever they had in mind has been postponed until June, at any rate.

When the jurors arrived at the courthouse and convened in their room yesterday morning Dist.-Atty. Foley went before them. After being before them for some time, during which it was rumored that he was informing the jurors that a complaint of some kind must be lodged before them before they took matters into their own hands, the jurors filed into a vacant courtroom. Judge Williams left the session where he was presiding and went before the grand jurors. 

Judge Williams said during the course of his remarks: 'Mr. Foreman and gentlemen. I take this occasion as you step in here mainly because of what I have seen in the headlines of the daily papers. I thought perhaps it was my duty to give you a little further instruction as to what I conceive to be the duties of a grand jury. I have no question but what you were adequately charged at the beginning of your term.

The grand jury is, of course, an adjunct of the court; it is an independent body, though under the general supervision of the court and its duty is to investigate alleged crimes and return indictments where they feel that crime has been committed. 

Ordinarily you deal with matters which are presented to you through the district attorney's office. It is wise that that should be the method, because the district attorney has the means for investigating crime, and has the personnel to present those matters to the grand jury.

It is never wise to indulge in haste in prosecutions. I believe it to be the custom in this state for district attorneys, as a rule, not to present matters to a grand jury unless there has first been a preliminary hearing in the lower court. That is the general rule. It is not a universal rule. There may be instances where a defendant has not been apprehended and where it is necessary to obtain a secret indictment for the purpose of apprehending the defendant. But ordinarily it is better to have a preliminary hearing in the lower court and then have the case bound over for the consideration of the grand jury by a magistrate of the lower court, or else to take it up in some other phases after there has been a finding on some matters by the lower court magistrate. 

There is, however, a class of cases where a grand jury is warranted in considering the matter on their own initiative. If you, Mr. Foreman, were out on some street in Boston and saw a crime committed, if no action was taken by the public authorities, it would be your duty to present the evidence which you yourself had obtained through your own senses to your fellows in the grand jury and take action. 

And the same would obtain if any other members of the grand jury obtained such evidence. In other words, gentlemen, where you know a crime has been committed and no action has been taken it is the duty of the grand jury to go ahead, as I say, on its own initiative.

There may be cases where you have not the evidence of your own senses, and the case which I have seen discussed in the daily papers may be such a case. But the rule is that the grand jury should act only on knowledge. It may not be personal knowledge such as the case I suggested to you-but it should be knowledge of the existence of real evidence. You should not act, in other words, simply on rumors and reports. For instance, Mr. Foreman, suppose, in the vicinity where you live there were rumors around that there was a house of ill fame somewhere there, and it was creating a good deal of talk in the vicinity, and you had

vised that the grand jury should "proceed with caution," and intimated that the grand jury should be slow to investigate matters not brought to its attention by the prosecuting officers. The second inroad on the former prerogative of the grand jury indicates that the preferable practice is that the instigation of all criminal charges should arise by complaint in the lower court.310 

Before this ruling and this decision, custom and practice had destroyed much of the ancient glory of the grand jury. By those who still have supreme confidence in the jury system and trace the evils of that system to the laws and customs which permit minor officers with personal, financial, or political prejudices to select those whose names shall be placed on jury lists, and to the usurping of the important powers of a grand jury by other bodies, these changes are approved with hesitation. Here, as in reason to believe that there was a house of ill fame existing there, you would not be justified as a member of the grand jury or as the foreman of the grand jury to summon in all the people in that vicinity and inquire of them if they knew of the existence of such a house, because you have no evidence to go by at the start.

Now, the same is true in regard to the situation which has apparently developed here. You have heard rumors, you understand they are reports. I venture to say that you probably have no real evidence at the moment as to what has transpired, if anything. You should wait until such evidence is obtained before you take action. 

It is perfectly clear in my mind that

I should give you that advice as a matter of law.

There has been a hearing, I understand, before some commission which has been authorized to conduct a hearing. If, after having seen the full report of that commission and after having obtained a transcript of the evidence you find that there is real evidence of the commission of any crime or crimes, of course it is the duty of some one to prosecute. That some one should be the district attorney; he is the one who is entrusted by the people of this community to sift the evidence, to collect the evidence, to weigh the evidence and to proceed. But if you find that the district attorney is negli gent, does not do what you conceive to be his duty on evidence which you know to exist, then it is your duty to proceed if you see fit to do so. But you should wait, first of all, until you find that there is to be real evidence, and, secondly-if I may give you this word of advice, in the interest of the orderly conduct of affairs in this city -I think you should wait until the district attorney had had an equal op portunity to discover what the evidence is and proceed if he sees fit to do so. 

What I first spoke of as a matter of law, in other words, I am telling you what I conceive to be the duties of a grand jury. The second matter that I referred to, in reference to giving the district attorney a chance to sift whatever evidence may exist, I am simply giving you by way of advice, because we are all interested in the orderly conduct of criminal procedure in this commonwealth, and it has been found that it is better to put the responsibility on the official who is elected by the people of the district for him to bear the responsibility. If for any reason you think you should go ahead because he has not done what you think he should have done, then it is your duty to proceed, and as we say in railroad circles, I think it is a good time to proceed with caution.''

3. Petit jury-a. Duty to hear and determine facts. "In a trial to a jury, the jurors are the proper arbiters of questions of fact other than the incidental matters of fact involved in the detail of trial. It is only in rare instances that the judge can assume to decide them, and only when no other decision is legally possible on the evidence." 814 "When a party has the burden of proving the affirmative of a proposition, it is usually for the jury to decide whether that burden is sustained; and, even when the evidence is not contradicted, it is for them to say whether they will believe it.” 315 The jury is to listen attentively to the evidence.816 If the jurors fail to recall the evidence, the court is under no obligation to tell them what the evidence was and their request that the judge inform them as to whether a particular witness had contradicted certain statements may be refused.317 The court, however, may read to them a second time on their request certain interrogatories and the answers thereto.818 When the court summarized the evidence in his charge or at any other time in the jury's presence, he should instruct them that their recollection of the evidence and not his is to govern. 819 

Whether the burden of proof has been sustained usually is for the jury.320 Briefly the duty of the jury is "to find the facts by weighing all the evidence." 821

"In a trial to a jury, the jurors are the proper arbiters of questions of fact other than the incidental matters of fact involved in the detail of trial. It is only in rare instances that the judge can assume to decide them, and only when no other decision is legally possible on the evidence. (Citing, O'Neill v. Middlesex & Boston Street Railway, 

244 Mass. 510.) The trial judge, like the appellate court, must consider that the jurors can give to contradictory evidence the construction most favorable to the party upon whom the burden of proof rests, and may refuse credit to evidence which he (often with greater experience and impartiality) regards as truthful and conclusive. It may be his duty both to submit the facts to the jury for their decision and to set aside the decision when given because it is contrary to the evidence and the weight of the evidence. Even though he would consider on the facts that one party should receive a verdict, yet he cannot order such verdict; and if there is any evidence to support a finding for the party with the burden of proof he must submit the case to the jury.368 Though he is convinced that the facts are such that should the jury find for a certain party he would set the verdict aside, yet he should submit the case to them.864 Whether if twenty-five reliable persons testify to a fact contradicted by only one, whom the trial court disbelieves, the trial court must supervise the jury's verdict and cause it to be set aside or recorded in favor of him in whose favor such preponderance appears, is a question raised but not decided.365 If a jury disagrees and disagreeing reports, the trial judge may instruct them further,366 and may charge that each may give some weight to the opinion of his fellows; 367 be sustained." 399 following. Agreement after jury has separated allowed. "The declaration in an action of tort by an administrator contained three counts, one for conscious suffering of the intestate, one for damage to his property and one for causing his death. Special questions were submitted to the jury on a 

Thursday relating to due care of the plaintiff, negligence of the defendant and damages, it being agreed by counsel that the answers to the questions should be regarded as a sealed verdict in that the formal opening of the verdicts one way or the other might be done when the jury reconvened on the next court day, which was Monday. 

The jury separated at eleven o'clock at night on Thursday. When court reconvened on Monday the foreman of the jury announced agreements on the answers to all the questions except one, which related to the damages to be assessed under the count for causing death. From the other answers it appeared that the jury had found that the intestate was in the exercise of due care and that the defendant was negligent. The foreman, in answer to an inquiry by the judge, stated that he thought that an agreement might be reached as to the unanswered question. 

Upon inquiry, the judge was informed that no member of the panel had talked with anybody in any manner about the The judge thereupon ordered the jury to return to their room and consider the unanswered question further. 

They did so and agreed upon an answer upon which as a basis the judge ordered a finding for the plaintiff upon the appropriate count of the declaration. 

Held, that the action of the judge was not an improper exercise of his discretion."

[5] Setting aside verdict. The court for just cause on proper procedure may set aside the whole or a part of a verdict.396 

This action lies within the discretionary power of the court and is considered heretofore.897 A court may give directions to the jury after a verdict is returned and before it is affirmed and recorded.398 It has been held error, however, in the Federal 

Court for a court to recall a jury after it has disagreed for a considerable time and ask the jurors how they were numerically divided.899 [6] Ordering judgment contrary to verdict. If a party has moved that a verdict be entered in his favor and the court, subject to exception, has denied this motion and has submitted the case to the jury, though the jury returns a verdict against the moving party the Supreme Judicial Court on exceptions in substance may grant the motion, upset the verdict, and order final judgment.400 This is in effect like a nunc pro tunc ruling on the motion. The trial court of course in such case, should the verdict be unsupported, on proper motion may set aside the verdict.401 So too by statute the court may ask the jury to grant the right to reverse its verdict if as a matter of law that verdict is wrong. 402 When such right is given, if error has appeared at the trial and the case on the facts established by the verdict justly should be disposed of by a ruling of law with a result contrary to the verdict, the court, without retrial, may reverse the jury's verdict and may enter a judgment.408 If rulings of law require a certain verdict, even after a case has been given to the jury and the jury has retired, the court at any time before the verdict is returned, affirmed, and recorded, may recall the jury and direct a proper verdict.404 When the jury have answered questions which involve the issue, in a manner that is

Counsel admits that defendant's purpose was to 'find out what his (W. D. Russell's) attitude was toward the defendants to be tried.' 

And that this (we are stating the effect of the counsel's contention) was only in preparation of a sinister purpose; that the defendants in the case did not wish to undertake, or to use the language of the indictment, did not 'want to pay money to any of the petit jurors sitting at the trial of said case unless they knew such petit jurors would favor their acquittal.' And this, counsel says, 'only amounted to a solicitation of a third person who did not accept or act in furtherance of such solicitation,' and 'could be interpreted only to be preparation for an 'endeavor' or 'attempt' to influence the juror, but falls far short of an actual endeavor to do so.' 

We think, however, that neither the contention nor the cases are pertinent to the section under review and upon which the indictment was based. 

Criminality does not get rid of its evil quality by the precautions it takes against consequences, personal or pecuniary. It is a somewhat novel excuse to urge that Russell's action was not criminal because he was cautious enough to consider its cost and be sure of its success. The section, however, is not directed at success in corrupting a juror, but at the 'endeavor' to do so. Experimental approaches to the corruption of a juror are the 'endeavor' of the section. Guilt is incurred by trialsuccess may aggravate, it is not a condition of it.

The indictment charges that defendant knew that William D. Russell was a petit juror, in the discharge of his duty as such juror, and therefore, an endeavor to corruptly influence him was within the section, though he was not yet selected or sworn. American Bar 

Ass'n Journal, May 1927, P. 220.

478 e. Jury's method of discerning facts-(1) Introductory. 

A jury is to procure its knowledge of the facts in a case from certain approved methods only. Jurors are not to conduct an inquest, or to go about to learn the truth by their own investigation. Any fact which is presented, is to be presented by an approved method of proof. Though jurors are to use their experience 479 to assist them in determining credibility, veracity, accuracy, and matters of common knowledge, and in establishing what are acts of the ordinary reasonably prudent man, yet they are not to employ their private knowledge of the character of a witness,480 or of other ordinary specific facts.481 If a juror has such knowledge which he desires to present, he should offer himself as a witness, 488

(3) Interpretation of inaccuracies-(a) Introductory. 

Though evidence presented verbally may not be perfectly clear, yet a witness by gesture, vocal or facial expression, or other outward sign may indicate what his meaning is; in interpreting such evidence, the jury may consider these and find that they clarify the ambiguous verbal statements.485 So though a witness is somewhat indefinite in his evidence the jury in some instances may find that a certain meaning was intended. Even positive statements as to time and distance may be considered inaccurate.486 Illustrations and contrasts follow. (b) Time. Statements of time are not always accurate.

They frequently are but estimates and juries may so consider them. The statement of a witness that four or five minutes elapsed during a certain interval need not be taken literally.487 

Computation in seconds, founded only on uncertain estimates made from judgment and memory, is hardly more than a scintilla of evidence to set against other more accurate testimony.488 

Even a statement of a witness that an act happened “in the winter" on modifying facts may be interpreted by the jury to have been intended as a statement that the act happened in the fall.489 When a date is to be fixed some range of inaccuracy the finding of a variance between the allegations contained in the specifications and the proof. Meaning of clause "Words to that effect." Danofsky v.

Boston El., 228 Mass. 97. Witness who fully testifies falsely. Jury may apply "falsus in uno falsus in omnibus." 

(Citing Commonwealth v. Wood, 11 

Gray 85, 93;

(j) Inconsistent testimony of a witness. If the testimony of a witness is inconsistent, the jury, subject to one limitation, may believe the truth of either inconsistency,507 or under the maxim "Falsus in uno falsus in omnibus," 508 it may reject, but is not obliged to reject, the whole.500 The one limitation referred to is this. If a party who testifies to inconsistencies finally adopts one of the inconsistencies as true, until he changes his testimony he cannot claim that the other inconsistency is true. 510 

In the absence of fraud or like matter the same is probably true of all witnesses who are not parties; in the absence of unusual circumstances the side calling the witness cannot rely on an inconsistency after the witness has clearly repudiated it.511 

Some allowance doubtless should be made for mistake, lack of clearness of memory, fear, or the excitement of the situation. 

As yet the extent of that allowance seems not defined. If a witness in full possession of his own free will and judgment, finally selects one of his inconsistencies as true the party who called him cannot rely on the truth of his other inconsistent testimony.512 This is not to be confused with the rule as to "prior consistent statements" made out of court.518 agreement, did not make this as their contract. (k) Negative evidence: Witness failing to observe: Evi dence that one inattentive did not hear or see. Usually evidence that one near the scene of an event did not hear certain sounds, cannot be taken by the jury as evidence that those sounds were not present.514 To render such evidence of probative value the fact that the witness was attentive, or that the sounds were such that they would have been heard by a person situated as was the witness must be established.515 The same general principle doubtless applies to failure to see inconspicuous articles. signing a contract, however, a person must be more observant.

mankind.555 "In trial of cases as in the ordinary affairs of life, it is often impossible to establish the connection between cause and effect with absolute certainty. But evidence which produces a moral conviction is sufficient. It is upon such conviction that men act in the important concerns of life and no greater certainty is required or attainable." 556 There is an exception in practice to the rule that the chain of circumstantial evidence must run unbroken to the exact cause. If negligence of the defendant is the issue and a result must have arisen from one of two negligent causes and both are attributable to the defendant, it is unnecessary to show which was the actual cause.557 If one of the two must have been the cause and if the defendant is responsible for either and both, his liability is sufficiently established. The same principle doubtless applies in contracts. 

A jury may be convinced by circumstantial evidence.558 To warrant conviction in a criminal case on such evidence the circumstances must be such as to produce a moral certainty of guilt, and to exclude any other reasonable hypothesis; the circumstances taken together, to warrant conviction, should be of a conclusive nature and tendency, leading on the whole to a satisfactory conclusion and producing in effect a reasonable and moral certainty that the accused and no one else committed the offense.559 When guilt is sought to be established by circumstantial evidence if one of the circumstantial facts essential to the chain of evidence is inconsistent with the guilt of the accused, the continuity of the proof is broken and proof beyond a reasonable doubt by that set of circumstances is made impossible.560 When such is the case the accused is entitled to a ruling to that effect; but it by no means follows that the defendant must be found not guilty. There may be other evidence in the case from which guilt may be proved with the necessary certainty. So there may be facts which standing by themselves would be inconsistent with guilt, 555 Mady v. He is thus recognized by the statutes, as well as by the long established custom of the courts, as the one who presides over the deliberations of the jury. His duty in this regard requires a maintenance of orderly discussion and decision. While his power is no greater than that of any juror, he is by virtue of his office the first juryman, and the chief of the twelve for the purpose of communicating with the court. He is the legally recognized voice of the jury. Through him the jury speaks. His signature alone is appended to verdicts and other papers in which the finding of the jury is expressed, and not that of each juror. In most instances the assent of the other members of the panel to all conclusions expressed in open court is asked formally, in order that there may be no mistake. Not infrequently questions are put orally to the jury by the presiding justice.
