The jury should recall the material evidence, give due weight to the argument of counsel, follow the law as given by the court, eliminate all prejudice, and if possible reach a fair, consistent and unanimous verdict.

The jury is not bound to believe evidence even though it is uncontradicted.571 It may believe a witness in part and disbelieve him in part.572

The jurors should listen attentively to the argument of their fellow jurors and give due weight to their opinions and reasons for their opinions.578 They should listen with open minds willing to be convinced by fair argument.574 A charge which tends to lead a juror to follow his own judgment exclusively is unsound and inapposite. On this subject the law in Massachusetts is exact, and the leading case which has been said to have been regarded as "going nearly if not quite to the extreme limit," 575 so exactly sets the law that a charge varying from it but in slight detail may constitute cause for reversal of a verdict.578 The charge in that case with criticising opinions 597 is set out in the notes.

597 The following from the Massa-

chusetts Quarterly, May, 1925, page 26, and following sets out an editorial of the Boston Post, June 3, 1925, the charge in Commonwealth v. Tuey, and quotations from the text of similar cases:- "The minority Juror and Judge Hoar's

Charge in Commonwealth V. Tuey. 

(From the Boston Post, June 3, 1925.) 

The case of Juror Andrew, who stood out for conviction in the Macri murder case at New Haven, has attracted wide attention. The Connecticut Bar Asso ciation has severely denounced the treatment accorded Mr. Andrew in the attempt to force him to agree with the other jurors.

The State of Massachusetts is in a peculiar position on this very subject of coercing jurors.

Many years ago, in the case of the 

Commonwealth v. Tuey, Judge Hoar, one of our most eminent jurists, was annoyed over the failure of the jury to agree on а conviction within a reasonable time. He sent for the jury and in carefully chosen language instructed them that it was the duty of the minority to consider carefully the arguments of the majority, and, without surrendering their personal right of opinion, to see if they could not agree with the majority.

That instruction was effective. The jury looked upon it for what it was, a plain intimation that the majority was probably right.

The Supreme Court of that day upheld this instruction.

Since then, at various times, judges have called in balky juries and read the decision to them. Many times it has resulted in verdicts when juries seemed hopelessly deadlocked.

Our Supreme Court has, however, been extremely uneasy over this ruling as laid down by Judge Hoar. It has not hesitated to characterize it as 'going to the extreme limit' and as a decision which 'many able jurists think exceeds the limit of judicial instruction.' 

So touchy are the Supreme Court judges over it that other Superior Court judges who attempted to put in their own words the gist of Judge Hoar's ruling have suffered reversal at the hands of the Supreme Court. Only the very remarkable ingenuity of language possessed by Judge Hoar has kept his ruling the law of the State up to the present. 

There are times when a stubborn juror performs a most valuable service. 

Our jury system is based on the individual opinions of 12 men on the evidence at the trial. No man should be asked to surrender his honest opinion merely to prevent the jury from reporting a disagreement. A disagreement is very often a most unsatisfactory outcome of a trial, but an agreement forced by the coercion of the minority is a repugnant one. 

The Massachusetts ruling, as the 

Supreme Court has twice remarked, 'goes to the extreme limit.' It seems, to the layman, to offer too much support to jury majorities. To lawyers and judges the careful language of Judge

Hoar and the profound skill with which he avoided the direct language (which would have meant a reversal) may seem reasonable.

Still it is quite easy to conceive the effect of it on men unlearned in the law and to realize how greatly it tends to weaken the position of a minority juror, however firmly he is convinced he is right."

NOTE. 

"There is no question that a juror who has a real opinion and is strong enough to stand by it performs a valuable service in the community. The public realization of this fact is, and has been, the reason for our constitutional requirement that a verdict shall be unanimous instead of the provisions for majority verdicts which have been adopted elsewhere, but, in view of the editorial criticism above quoted from the 'Post' of the instruction given by Judge Hoar to the jury in Com. v. Tuey, (8 Cush. 1) the full report of that instruction as it is given in the report of the case is here quoted for the purpose of discussion. The charge was as follows: 

'The only mode, provided by our constitution and laws for deciding questions of fact in criminal cases, is by the verdict of a jury. In a large proportion of cases, and perhaps, strictly

speaking, in all cases, absolute certainty cannot be attained or expected. Although the verdict to which a juror agrees must of course be his own verdict, the result of his own convictions, and not a mere acquiescence in the conclusion of his fellows, yet, in order to bring twelve minds to a unanimous result, you must examine the questions submitted to you with candor, and with a proper regard and deference to the opinions of each other. You should consider that the case must at some time be decided; that you are selected in the same manner, and from the same source, from which any future jury must be; and there is no reason to suppose that the case will ever be submitted to twelve more intelligent, more impartial, or more competent to decide it, or that more or clearer evidence will be produced on the one side or the other. And with this view, it is your duty to decide the case, if you can conscientiously do so. In order to make a decision more practicable, the law imposes the burden of proof on one party or the other, in all cases. In the present case, the burden of proof is upon the commonwealth to establish every part of it, beyond a reasonable doubt; and if, in any part of it, you are left in doubt, the defendant is entitled to the benefit of the doubt, and must be acquitted. But, in conferring together, you ought to pay proper respect to each other's opinions, and listen, with a disposition to be convinced, to each other's arguments. And, on the one hand, if much the larger number of your panel are for a conviction, a dissenting juror should consider whether a doubt in his own mind is a reasonable one, which makes no impression upon the minds of so many men, equally honest, equally intelligent with himself, and who have heard the same evidence, with the same attention, with an equal desire to arrive at the truth, and under the sanction of the same oath. And, on the other hand, if a majority are for acquittal, the minority ought seriously to ask themselves, whether they may not reasonably, and ought not to doubt the correctness of a judgment, which is not concurred in by most of those with whom they are associated; and distrust the weight or sufficiency of that evidence which fails to carry conviction to the minds of their fellows.'

The propriety of this charge came before the full bench of the Supreme 

Judicial Court upon the defendant's objections after a verdict of 'Guilty' 

in 1851. The court then consisted of: 

Lemuel Shaw, Chief Justice; Theron 

Metcalf, Richard Fletcher, and George 

T. Bigelow (later chief justice). The opinion was written by Mr. Justice

Bigelow and was concurred in by the other judges as follows: 'The defendant objects to the instructions given to the jury in this case, on the ground, that they were equivalent to a direction, on the part of the court, to a minority of the jury to yield their own opinions and judgment to the views of the majority, and render a verdict in conformity therewith; or, in other words, that a dissenting juror was bound to take into consideration the opinions of his fellows, as an element by which his own convictions were to be controlled. But we do not so understand the purport and effect of the language used by the judge who tried the case. The instructions went no further, than to say, that if any of the jury differed, in their views of the evidence, from a large number of their fellows, such difference of opinion should induce the minority to doubt the correctness of their own judgments, and lead them to a re-examination and closer scrutiny of the facts in the case, for the purpose of revis ing and reconsidering their preconceived opinions. In this view, the court did nothing more than to present to the minds of the dissenting jurors a strong motive to unanimity. 

Upon a careful consideration of these instructions, we are clearly of opinion, that so far from being improper, or of a nature to mislead, they were entirely sound, and well adapted to bring to the attention of the jury one of the means by which they might be safely guided in the performance of their duty. A proper regard for the judg ment of other men will often greatly aid us in forming our own. In many of the relations of life, it becomes a

duty to yield and conform to the opinions of others, when it can be done without a sacrifice of conscientious convictions; more especially is this a duty, when we are called on to act with others and when dissent on our part 'may defeat all action and materially affect the rights and interests of third parties. Such is the rule of duty constantly recognized and acted on by courts of justice. They not only form their opinions, but reconsider, revise, and modify their own declared judgments, by the aid and in the light of the decisions of other tribunals. But this could not be done if it were not per- 

Imitted to them to doubt and correct their opinions, when they were found to differ from those of other men, who have had equal opportunities of arriving at sound conclusions with themselves. 

The jury room is, surely, no place for pride of opinion, or for espousing and maintaining, in the spirit of controversy, either side of a cause. The single object to be there effected is to arrive at a true verdict; and this can only be done by deliberation, mutual concession and a due deference to the opinions of each other. By such means and such only, in a body where unanimity is required, can safe and just results be attained; and without them, the trial by jury, instead of being an essential aid in the administration of justice, would become a most effectual obstacle to it. (8 Cushing 2–3).' 

When the instruction of Judge Hoar is read and considered in the light of the foregoing opinion sustaining it, is there really any sound reason on which even laymen should criticize it? The theory of the jury system as it has developed, both in England and in this country as one of the free institutions in a free country, is that the jurymen have intelligence and independence enough to consider the evidence and form their own opinion.

As a practical matter, does not the criticism in the editorial above quoted in the language of Chief Justice Taney of the Supreme Court of the United States in Mitchell v. Harmony, 13 How. 

420 'question the (jurors') intelligence and independence; which can not be brought into doubt without taking from that tribunal the confidence and respect which so justly belongs to it in questions of fact'?

While it is true that Judge Hammond in Highland Foundry Co. v. N. Y., N. 

H. & H. R. R., 199 Mass. at 407 stated that the case of Com. v. Tuey 'generally has been regarded by the profession as going nearly, if not quite, to the extreme limit' that remark even if correct, is not a criticism but simply a description and while it is also true, of course, that in charging a jury in such a matter a judge is always 'treading on delicate ground' and must choose his words with care, yet, as 

Judge Hammond also said, 'perhaps no case in our reports is more familiar to the trial bar than Com. v. Tuey.'

The fact that it has stood the test of about 75 years of practice indicates 

Judge Hoar's sound practical sense in his choice of words. Similar instructions taken from Judge Hoar's charge and used in a criminal case in the

Federal Courts, Allen v. U. S., 164 U. S. 

at p. 501, were unanimously sustained by the Supreme Court of the United 

States in 1896. That court said in the opinion by Mr. Justice Brown: 

'While, undoubtedly, the verdict of the jury should represent the opinion of each individual juror, it by no means follows that opinions may not be changed by conference in the jury-room.

The very object of the jury system is to secure unanimity by a comparison of views, and by arguments among the jurors themselves. It certainly cannot be the law that each juror should not listen with deference to the arguments and with a distrust of his own judg ment, if he finds a large majority of the jury taking a different view of the case from what he does himself. It cannot be that each juror should go to the jury-room with a blind determination that the verdict shall represent his opinion of the case at that moment; or, that he should close his ears to the arguments of men who are equally honest and intelligent as himself. There was no error in these instructions.'''

"The jury room is, surely, no place for pride of opinion or for espousing and maintaining, in the spirit of controversy, either side of a cause. The single object to be there effected is to arrive at a true conviction and this can only be done by deliberaration, mutual concession, and a due deference to the opinion of each other. By such means and such means only, in a body where unanimity is required, can safe and just results be attained; and without them, the trial by jury, instead of being an essential aid in the administration of justice would become a most effectual obstacle to it." 599

Improprieties by jurors and juries. Not every slight impropriety by a juror or by a jury requires the declaration of a mistrial, or the granting of a new trial.628 Much in this respect rests in the discretion of the trial court.624 Many matters which involve improprieties by jurors and juries have been taken up heretofore.625 A juror's impartiality,626 his alleged insanity, drunkenness,627 or lack of qualifications,628 his relationship to, or employment by, a party,629 or his interest in the outcome of the case, 680 his bias,681 or his crystalized opinion formed from facts not in evidence, 682 his acting under duress,683 coercion,634 During the deliberations of the jury, one juryman complained of being sick from indigestion and heart trouble.

The court sent for a physician and instructed him under appropriate conditions to attend the ailing juror and to advise whether he was able to continue further consideration of the case. The physician reported to the court that the juror had substantially recovered and could in his opinion continue further consideration of the case. An officer in charge of the jury inquired thereafter about once an hour during the remainder of the night whether the juror was able to go on, and was told that he was. The judge found as a fact upon all the evidence that the juror was able to perform his duty. In all this there was no error. The hypothetical question to the physician on crossexamination at the hearing on the motions for new trial was rightly excluded.

A court may submit special questions in civil cases, and under certain circumstances, in criminal cases, to the jury.668 The verdict should contain answers to these.669 If the jury fails to agree on one issue, this is not the same as a verdict against the person who has the burden of proof; it is like a disagreement.670 If the jury does not specifically answer one question, but its answer implies that it intended to answer in the affirmative, the court may accept the implication.871 It is similar to a blank left in a verdict, which the court and parties have accepted as immaterial error.672 If the answers to the questions enable the court in correcting errors of law, to ascertain the true damages,678 enter a final judgment without retrial, this may be done. or to (4) Verdict showing evidence admitted not admissible.

If a jury in answering questions or in returning a separate verdict on several counts, answers inconsistently, the verdict as returned cannot have a meaning.682 

The court on its own motion may set aside the inconsistent answers.688 Illustrations of inconsistency are when a defendant tried by the same jury for larceny of chattels and for receiving of the same chattels knowing them to have been stolen, is found guilty on both charges. He cannot be guilty of both offenses, hence the verdict is inconsistent.684 The pleadings will be looked to, to determine the identity of the charge.685 In a civil action the same principle applies. "It is true that where there are two counts which the evidence shows to be inconsistent, a verdict of guilty as to each is inconsistent and ground for reversal."' 686 

There are, however, apparent modifications of the rule. An illustrative case was submitted to a jury on three counts and the jury found for the defendant on two and for the plaintiff on the third; apparently not only the pleading and verdict were looked 680 Compare Chapter 1, numbers 108 to 130. A presiding judge who has submitted special questions to the jury, has discretionary power to set aside answers of the jury which are clearly inconsistent; it cannot be said which of them is true without entering upon the province of the jury. "On the motion of the plaintiff the judge set aside the answer of the jury to the fourth question as unwarranted and not responsive. As the answer to the sixth question was clearly inconsistent with the answers to the ninth and tenth questions, and it could not be said which was true without entering upon the province of the jury, the judge properly set aside the three answers. This action was within the discretionary power of the court, even upon its own motion.' (Citing, Reilly v. Boston Elevated Ry., 206 Mass. 53;

The first count was on an account annexed for commission on sales to a certain company; the second count was for breach of an alleged contract to pay commission on all sales to the same company; and the third count was on an agreement of the plaintiff to disclose purchasers to the defendant in consideration of a promised commission, under which, as alleged, he disclosed the same purchaser. The jury returned a verdict for the defendant on the first and second counts and for the plaintiff on the third count. The court in interpreting the meaning of the third count apparently looked to the plaintiff's brief which was in part as follows: "it, [the plaintiff] is entitled to be paid the fair value of its services as broker and agent in disclosing and procuring a purchaser of the defendant's goods." The court said, "The plaintiff under the first or second count might have recovered if the jury had believed either that there was an express contract or an implied contract between the parties for a commission. The verdict for the defendant on those counts conclusively establishes that there was no express or implied contract for the payment of a commission to the plaintiff on the sales here in question. The verdicts for the defendant on the first two counts are incompatible with any liability on the part of the defendant on the third count.' "The testimony of the plaintiff's only witness fails to establish any ground of liability on the third count. The plaintiff cannot recover on any theory of unjust enrichment." The court distinguishes the case from several others, declares that a verdict should have been ordered on the third count and under General Laws, chapter 231, sections 122 and 123, orders final judgment for the defendant, without retrial.687

The fact that a verdict is larger than the total claimed in either of two counts of a declaration does not show the verdict erroneous. 

Hence when a declaration to recover value of professional services was in two counts, an account annexed and quantum meruit, there was no error in the fact that the verdict was larger than the total claimed in either count. I. Attorney's duty to his client: Fees. An attorney, in serving his client, acts in a highly fiduciary capacity.¹ Judges, arbitrators, juries, and other arbiters of fact, as stated above, must be impartial; but an attorney owes the duty to his client of protecting his client's honorable and honest interests to the exclusion of all other persons. He must be fair with his client, disclose all material circumstances and not take advantage of his fiduciary relationship. Even after the case is tried and when fees are to be set the fiduciary relationship usually exists.5

If an attorney in deducting his fee from funds in his hands, refuses to turn over the amount justly due his client until the client signs a release, if the client to receive a portion of the funds signs a release under seal which approves the deducted fee, he may at his option, if the fee is excessive, set aside the release and procure a fair accounting. An attorney who conducts a case for an infant or insane person who sues through his next friend or guardian ad litem, when he receives the proceeds of the suit has the usual lien against those proceeds for the fees and expenses of that suit." He may retain a sufficient sum to satisfy this lien. If the deduction is fair he apparently stands the same against the infant or lunatic as against a normal adult. 

If the fee is excessive and the adult voluntarily pays it, if all the facts are disclosed and there is no actual fraud, the settlement is binding. With an infant or lunatic regardless of any agreement with the infant or his next friend or guardian ad litem, the fee must be fair.8

An attorney, regardless of who hires him or who pays him, must act primarily and without negligence for the interest of his client. Of course he cannot in the same controversy, without the active actual consent of all concerned, act for adverse interest.10 When there are several controversies not in any way connected with one another, there is no rule of law which requires that an attorney who acts for one party in a suit, cannot made to her; but because of the position taken by the defendant and the statements made, she was not free to act, but was compelled to accept the defendant's terms. As a matter of fact, the judge was warranted in finding that the release was subject to the condition imposed by the defendant and was not fairly and honestly obtained; there was no error of law in the ruling given.'

259 act for his adversary in a controversy which is in no way connected with that suit.11 In such matters much must depend on the amount involved, the bitterness of the contests, the animosities of the parties, the size of the community where all live, and perhaps the actual confidence placed in the attorney by both parties. The better plan in all such matters is for the attorney to procure the consent of his original client before he takes the suit of an adversary. An attorney's acting in one case for a party against whom he acts in another pending suit, is looked on with suspicion,-it is a practice not to be encouraged.12 

II. Attorney's duty to court. An attorney, as an officer of the court, owes the duty to act in all matters with respect for the court, with honesty, and in obedience to the law.18 In the trial of cases he should avoid even the appearance of courting favor with the trial court or with the jurors.14 An attorney should not seek to influence a jury in any way but by the presentation of his facts in open court, by fair conduct with his adversary and by fair and logical argument. 

III. Attorney's attitude toward the jury. The right of an attorney to investigate the qualifications of the jurors out of court, cannot be questioned,15 but in that investigation and in his attitude in and about the court room he should take precautions that his acts cannot be taken as acts of coercion or duress,16 and that they are not mistaken as attempts to curry favor or indirectly to influence a juror or prospective juror.17 

The method of examination of proposed jurors before they are sworn and the right of an attorney to challenge for cause or otherwise is treated elsewhere.18

IV. Questioning attorney's right to act. If the right of an attorney to appear for a party is demanded, "if such attorney declares that he has been duly authorized to appear by an application made directly to him" by his alleged client "or by some person whom he believes to have been authorized to employ him, such declaration shall be evidence of such authority." 19 Rules frequently require that objection to authority to appear shall be filed within a certain limited time.20 The methods of raising questions of an attorney's authority to appear are considered elsewhere.21 

V. Conducting of the case-A. Opening-1. Generally. 

When the jury has been impanelled the attorney for the plaintiff, or other party who has the burden of proof opens the case. 

This is done by his first reading to the court and jury the pleadings.22

These pleadings of course are not evidence in favor of the pleader,28 but they pass by custom at least, if not by actual right, with the exhibits, to the jury.24 After this reading usually the attorney for the plaintiff in an opening, addresses the jury.25 

This opening is not an argument; it must not contain matters of argument. He states to the jury in general what the plaintiff expects to prove and defines the nature of the questions involved.28 An opening should contain no more. When the plaintiff or other party with the burden of proof has presented his side of the case and has rested, the defendant or respondent before presenting his evidence may make an opening. The 

Superior Court, however "in its discretion may permit a defendant to make an opening statement to the court or jury before any evidence is put in." 28

261 2. Length of opening. By rules of the Superior Court the court limits the time to be consumed by the opening to fifteen minutes; for cause shown the court may extend the time.29 

3. Reference in opening to inadmissible evidence or improper matter. In an opening a party outlines his case. Usually he may state specifically what evidence he intends to present. If he refers in the opening to inadmissible evidence, within the court's discretion he may be instructed to omit such reference from his opening; if the admissibility of the evidence is questionable, the same applies.30 The adversary unless the court directs to the contrary may forthwith object to any objectionable part of the opening; on such objection the court should cause a correction of any error and by proper instructions to the jury should fully protect the interest of all parties.81 A withdrawal or disclaimer of the objectionable statement by the speaker, may be sufficient to remedy the error. The court in such case doubtless may declare a mistrial.33 In an opening, remarks which accuse the adversary or his counsel of knowledge of disputed facts, even if not improper in the sense that they call for a judicial rebuke, yet are not in good taste and the jury should be instructed to disregard them.84 82

263 46 c. Ordering verdict on opening. There is no doubt but that in proper cases the trial court after a party who has the burden of proof has presented in his opening fully the facts which he intends to prove, may expedite justice by ruling, without listening to any evidence, that that party is not entitled to recover. 

Apparently he may do so in spite of Rule 44 of the Superior Court, on his own motion.48 There is one apparent limit on this right,—namely that if the pleadings show a clear cause of action in the party's favor, without more than a mere inadvertent insertion or omission of material facts in the opening, the court cannot so rule.19 Doubtlessly if the party either actually or impliedly admits that the only facts which he will present are those in his opening, and the court concludes that as a matter of law these will not sustain the burden of proof and make out a case, or a defense to a prima facie case, the court, regardless of pleadings may so rule.50 If the parties, by carefully reducing to writing the opening, and by permitting the court to study it and by studying it themselves as if the only questions in the case were the questions of law raised thereby treat the opening as an embodiment of the whole case, this will be sufficient to indicate that the opening as embodied in the written statement is a statement of the case which supersedes the technical pleadings.51 Furthermore the opening may confirm the pleadings which indicate that parties are improperly joined. B. Order of presentation of facts at large-1. Generally. 

The usual order of presenting the case at large is for the plaintiff after his opening to present his case in chief, to prove the necessary allegations of his declaration. When this is done he rests. The defendant then presents his side of the case,-his denial of the plaintiff's facts, his evidence of new matter set as a defense or set off, in his answer or declaration in set off. On his resting the plaintiff proceeds in rebuttal. This is followed by the defendant's rejoinder. This usually ends the evidence and the parties finally rest. Written requests for rulings or motions for directed verdicts, if any, are then presented to the court, and usually discussed. If the case is to go to the jury then the defendant argues to the jury; he is followed by the plaintiff. 

The court next charges the jury and at the close thereof the exhibits are presented to the jury and the jury retires.59 The order of this procedure doubtless may be varied in the court's proceeded against the other defendants without amendment. Taft v. Church, 162 Mass. 527, 533, 164 Mass. 504; Lee v. Blodget, above.

265 discretion. The general rule is that a party while, or before, his part of the case is first open, must present his facts if they become competent and necessary to sustain the declaration or answer; a party need not anticipate new matters which may appear in a defense or rebuttal 61 

2. Evidence offered out of order: Effect. The court has con siderable discretion in determining the order of presentation of evidence.62 During the presentation of the plaintiff's direct case all matter other than that which pertains to the direct case may be excluded.68 Hence, if, while the plaintiff's direct case is open, the defendant seeks in cross examination to bring out new matter set forth in and made material by his answer, the court in its discretion may exclude the question. If the plaintiff in his direct case presents evidence which is a part of his rebuttal he may thereby waive his right again to present like facts in rebuttal.65 So when in an action for the price of goods sold under warranty if the defense is breach of warranty, the ordinary order of proof permits the defendant for the first time in his case to raise the question of breach of warranty; the plaintiff in rebuttal then meets this defense.66 If, however, the plaintiff attempts to prove in his direct case that there was no breach of warranty, he may be precluded from presenting this defense again in rebuttal.67 Likewise in an action for breach of warranty, though the defense of breach of warranty is barred because the defendant, the buyer, did not seasonably complain to the seller of the breach of warranty, yet the plaintiff, if he in his direct case has attempted to prove that there was no breach of warranty, has been held to have waived the lack of complaint.

5. Result of failure to object: Objectionable evidence not objected to-a. Generally. If a party has failed to object to objectionable evidence to permit him after the close of the evidence to raise a question of the admissibility or of the probative value of the evidence admitted would tend unfairly to take advantage of his adversary.102 Failure to object to such evidence, waives its inadmissibility.108 To this there is probably an exception. If the evidence admitted without objection, does not disclose a cause of action or a defense which is within the pleadings, that evidence may be disregarded.104 There is, however, an exception to this exception. If a case is tried without regard to pleadings the court may refuse to consider the pleadings in passing on such evidence at such late time.105 So the result subject, however, to exception,106 seems to be that if evidence is admitted without objection, after the evidence is closed the court cannot instruct the jury to disregard the evidence, or limit its purpose or probative effect.107 A request for ruling as to the immateriality of evidence not objected to, where offered generally 108 should be refused.109 Objectionable evidence ad-

That a party, by facts which are inadmissible under the rules of evidence, has proved his case and then has objected to his adversary's proving by evidence of the same nature, his case, has called from the court a comment.185 If a proponent produces in the proof of his case facts inadmissible under the rules of evidence, may his opponent prove in his defense like facts which violate the same rule of evidence? Here is a conflict.186 In Massachusetts the rule has been thus stated. "The question then arises, how far the admission of incompetent and irrelevant evidence offered by one party, to which no objection is taken, renders it competent for the opposite party to introduce evidence of a similar character. 

There certainly must be some limit beyond which parties cannot be permitted to go, in extending issues of fact and bringing into a case matters which have no essential bearing on its real merits. 

Without indicating a general rule applicable to all cases of this nature, we think it may be safely said that a party should not be allowed to go farther than to prove facts which have a direct tendency to contradict and control the irrelevant or incompetent evidence which his adversary has introduced into the case. To this extent, it may be properly held that the latter has waived the strict rule of law applicable to such evidence, and is estopped from objecting to the proof of facts, by the opposite party, which can be properly deemed to be contradictory or in rebuttal of those offered by himself. It seems to us that the plaintiff was allowed to transcend this limit at the trial, in the introduction of evidence to which the defendant objected. He was not confined to disproof of the fact that he had charged the defendant with passing counterfeit money, which was the only ground of provocation which the latter had attempted to establish. The plaintiff was allowed to go much further, and to show the distinct and independent fact that the defendant had large sums of money in his possession, which he would take out in papers and show to persons about him, to the amount of several thousand dollars at a time. This was an irrelevant and immaterial fact, which not only had no bearing on the true issue between the parties, but did not tend to contradict or control the evidence

It is said by high authority "No one has doubted that if the opponent duly objected and was erroneously overruled in the first instance, he could not claim to present similar inadmissible facts because his objection will save him, on appeal, from any harm which may accrue and he needs no protection. But if he did not object and except he has no such protection, and the question then arises whether he can protect himself by retorting in kind.189

It has been said more recently in Massachusetts that if inadmissible evidence without the adversary's fault is admitted without objection the remedy is not to meet it by further inadmissible evidence, but to move to strike out the inadmissible evidence.140

The general principle now under discussion doubtless applies only to cases where inadmissible facts have been admitted; it cannot be taken to mean that the method or proof required by the rules of evidence, can be lightly waived. Because the plaintiff without objection of the defendant has proved his case by hearsay, does not mean that the defendant may prove his case over the plaintiff's objection by hearsay.141 Statute might allow this, but in the absence of statute or a clear waiver the rules of evidence are not to be lightly abrogated. f. D. Offer of proof-1. Introductory. On exceptions, the ex cepting party must show that he has suffered injury by the court's adverse ruling. 143 Generally a party's secret and undisclosed intent does not assist him in showing error in another who is ignorant of his intent.144 In offering evidence admissible for purposes which are not clearly disclosed by the evidence itself or by the attendant circumstances,145 the offering party, on objection to the evidence, unless such act is waived,148 should disclose those purposes.147 Thus disclosing the purposes for which the evidence is material is called an offer of proof. Failure to make an offer of proof frequently will result in exceptions which fail to show injury to the excepting party. If an offer of proof which would show the evidence admissible has not been made, no injury is shown.148 

2. Necessity of offer of proof-a. When required. When evidence is objected to and about to be rejected, unless the materiality of the evidence is apparent without an offer of proof,149 if no offer of proof is made and the evidence is rejected, no exception will be sustained.150 b. When not required. To preserve valid exceptions to a wrongful exclusion of evidence no offer of proof is required in the following instances: (1) When the question which is objected to shows in itself what the expected answer would be, and that that answer is material; 151 (2) when the attendant circumstances are such that the materiality of the question is evident;152 (3) and when the court by its attitude or direct statement

3. Time of offer. An offer of proof should be made as soon as objection to a question is made. Strictly it should be made before the court rules on admissibility. Offer of proof is a matter of right and the court by a quick ruling should not be permitted to cut off an opportunity to make such offer. If such ruling is made before the proponent has the opportunity to make his offer, he should except and ask that the ruling be left open until he makes his offer of proof. If the court refuses this he should again except. He should again ask in substance the same question and on objection make his offer of proof. The offer of proof is usually oral but the court doubtless may require that it be in writing.155 Under any circumstances the offer of proof should be in before the evidence is closed; however even here apparently the court has discretion.156 

4. Waiver of offer: Offer must be of actual testimony of a witness called. The offer should be made to present actual testimony; the witness should be called and the question asked

5. Substance of offer-a. Generally. Though the degree of exactness of the offer may vary with the circumstances,158 the general rule is that the offer of proof must embody all necessary facts to show relevancy and must not contain matter which is incompetent.159 b. Offer containing too much. If an offer is made as a whole, and sets forth facts which are admissible and facts which are inadmissible, if the court excludes the evidence there is no reversible error. The court of its own motion is not bound to separate the various parts of a complete offer of proof, and to admit evidence that is set forth in part only of the proof. An offer of proof should be so made that its parts are severable and separate from the whole. A reasonable opportunity to protect his rights should be given a proponent in such matter; but much lies in the court's discretion.160 If an offer of proof goes beyond the scope of the question it is objectionable.101 c. Offer containing too little. Frequently evidence offered is but a part of a chain of facts which render the present fact material.162 If an offer of proof does not contain a sufficient

164 Third count was to recover for certain bulbs at an agreed price. The defendant had received twenty-two thousand bulbs. These had been paid for except those covered by a promissory note and those covered by the third count. In defense to the third count the defendant offered to show that he tested about six thousand bulbs and found about half of them defective, and that the Edison Company tested certain bulbs by a scientific test and found them all defective. There was nothing to show that the evidence offered related to the bulbs mentioned in the third count. It did not appear that the plaintiff was the maker of the bulbs. They were of various candle power and design. The judge excluded the evidence. Held, that the exclusion was right, as the offer did not go far enough, there being no offer to show in what respect the bulbs tested were defective, or that the test was fairly applicable to the bulbs covered by the third count because of their size and kind; and so far as the offer of evidence went the six thousand bulbs examined might have been defective and yet all of those covered by the third count might have been perfect. A motion to strike out evidence is not a substitute for an objection.174 A party who fails to object will not be permitted as of right to allow an objectionable question to be answered, and then to have the answer stricken out on motion.175 As said above if a question on its face is inadmissible, objection to it, if possible, must be made when it is asked, not after it is answered.176 A party may move to strike out any inadmissible fact admitted without his fault.177 When the inadmissibility appears, the party should make his motion immediately.178 If he fails to do so, he may not be permitted to meet it by other like, inadmissible evidence.179

Exceptions and report. The only way to bring the materiality of evidence before the Supreme Judicial Court in a civil action at law is by exceptions or by report.208 In certain criminal matters by recent statute a new method is prescribed. 

In equity a question of evidence fairly on the record may be considered on appeal. Exceptions to rulings made in the presence of counsel should be taken immediately upon the announcement of the adverse ruling.205 So of a request for a report on matters of evidence in the district courts.206 The trial court probably may require that the exceptions, or at least the main facts on which exceptions depend, be reduced to writing at once.207 If the exception is to a ruling other than one made in the presence of counsel, a further time is allowed for excepting.208 A report in the superior court may be allowed after the time for filing exceptions has expired.209 An attorney should be careful that his bill of exceptions briefly sets out all matters material to establish the alleged erroneous ruling. It should show his seasonable objection and exception, the question objected to and the answer, and any relevant offer of proof, and the injury caused by the adverse ruling.

That a fair disclosure of all material evidence before trial is not wholly approved by the bar in this Commonwealth is evident from the evasive replies that frequently are filed in the answers to interrogatories, and to demands that certain facts be admitted. Perhaps this is because interrogatories are not always required to be answered fully and because failure to admit facts which one is called on to admit, does not carry sufficient penalty. The earlier history of the statutes which pertain to interrogatories, shows that the legislature with hesitation required a party to disclose his case;211 and even to-day the names of witnesses need be disclosed only in unusual cases,212 and the number of interrogatories which may be asked is limited.213 Some trial courts likewise even after the amendment of the statutes which pertain to interrogatories, though that amendment was approved by the Massachusetts Bar Association, and many leaders of the bar, were slow to encourage such method of procedure. Even the bar with hesitation took advantage of the great opportunities which this process offered. The courts of late have shown a tendency toward requiring a more fair disclosure of facts and circumstances, particularly during trial. Such is a requisite of a fair hearing and a fair disposal of cases. If a party now in answering interrogatories fails to insert matters which should be inserted he may find that his failure works against him and to his adversary's advantage.214 If during trial he does not clearly set out his contentions, and does not insist on them to the last, he may find that he has lost a perfectly good exception.215

L. Requests for rulings-1. Generally. After the evidence is closed and before arguments started either party may present to the court requests for rulings of law which the party desires covered in the charge.218 These requests to be proper must be applicable to the facts; a principle of law accurate in detail is not the proper subject for a request unless the facts of the case are such that they may fall within that principle.219 Subsequent findings 220 or rulings,221 or answers by the jury,222 may make a defendant's counsel moved to have stricken out the earlier evidence of the witness Violette and excepted to the denial of the motion. There is nothing to indicate that the Commonwealth was likely to be harmed by this change of attitude. No evidence had gone in upon the strength of the contention first advanced by the defendant, which for any reason rendered it unjust later to make a different contention. There was no such vacillation in the conduct of the defense as warranted the court in making any definite direction for the conduct of the trial as for example, that a final election could not be made until the evidence was closed. Indeed, this was not attempted by the court. 

A bald ruling was made that the defendant could not thus shift his ground during the trial. We are not able to construe the ruling as meaning anything else. The situation is in nowise different from the not unusual practice of withdrawing certain counts in an indictment after evidence in their support has been introduced. (Citing, Commonwealth v. Cody, 165 Mass. 133, 138.) It was said in Anthony v. Travis, 148 Mass. 53, 59, 60.-'Where a defendant has set up two distinct defenses, the fact that evidence had been admitted upon one defense which the court holds to be untenable, will not necessarily deprive the party of the right to maintain the other, because evidence irrelevant thereto was admitted in connection with the first defense.' While it well may be that counsel cannot change at will every position deliberately taken by them during the trial, it cannot be said in the case at bar that there was any reason why the counsel for the defendant might not make the change for which he asked leave. No final election was made. See Corbett v. B. & M. R. 

R., 219 Mass. 351, 357. The defendant's exception in this regard must be sustained. Although it has been suggested in argument that the defendant's change of position related solely to the testimony of Jacob Belford the ruling of the judge also may be said to relate to him. If any difference was made between the two Belford witnesses by the defendant, the same difference exists as to the ruling.” Commonwealth v. Retkovitz, 222 Mass. 245 at 252, 253.

3. Form of request. In form a request should be simple and clear. Many principles of law should not be consolidated in one request; each should be embodied in a separate and distinct request.282 If erroneous propositions of law are incorporated with other correct principles in a general request for rulings, the failure to give the ruling furnishes no ground for valid exception.288 

4. Substance of request-a. Generally: Singling out facts: 

Argumentative requests. A request should refer to principle of law, not of fact. The court is not required to emphasize facts by especially referring to some particular phase of the case and the facts in regard thereto as presented.234 A request should not be argumentative.285 It should not assume as true facts which are disputed or nonexistent.286 b. Reference to pleading. 5. Party bound by request. If a party asks a request and it is given in the terms asked he is bound and cannot complain that it is erroneous or that the jury might have misunderstood it.241

N. Argument-1. Generally. At the close of the evidence attorneys for the parties have the right to argue to the jury their cause. The defendant precedes; the plaintiff follows. The arguments should be confined to the issues of the case which have not been waived,258 facts of the case and their results under the law, and should not constitute an argument of the facts of other immaterial cases or matters.254

297 4. Objection to improper argument-a. Time of. An objection to an improper argument, it seems should be made at once.291 The speaker probably should be interrupted, an objection voiced and the objectionable part of the argument be pointed out.292

A delay in making the objection as stated above may be fatal; yet it has been held that an objection made during an intermission taken when argument is incomplete is seasonable.298 If the objector waits until the argument of his adversary has closed, though the court then may correct improprieties in the argument, yet if the court fails to do so the objector by his delay may have lost his right to a valid exception.294 

The requirement that a speaker who makes an objectionable argument must be interrupted at once should be subject to modification. To support this rule, to be sure, it may be said that if the argument is improper the speaker should be officially so informed while he still has opportunity to protect his rights in his argument; he should not be misled by inactivity into using his entire time for argument in setting forth a theory which the court will later rule inapposite. On the other hand, an attorney interrupted in his argument resents the interruption. It breaks his line of thought and the effect of the sequence of his logic. 

It disturbs his listeners and draws their attention from his general outline. Many of the more ethical members of the bar with hesitation interrupted their adversaries. Apart from the fact that the act in itself seems discourteous, they usually realize that the objectionable argument is caused by misapprehension, or a slip of the tongue, or of the memory. It is an act remembered by all concerned. The effect of such interruption, too, is emphatic. 

If the court sustains the objection his ruling weighs strongly against the speaker; if the court overrules the objection the jury and all others frequently must feel that the objector fears the

818 Defendant's counsel in an intermission in the plaintiff's closing argument excepted to statements of the plaintiff's counsel, and asked the presiding judge to instruct the jury to disregard them. In his charge the judge said, "During the argument of the counsel for the plaintiff he made certain statements to which the counsel for the defendant rose and objected. 

One was with reference to the right of the railway company to take your land by eminent domain; the other was with respect to your making law in the cases for Plymouth County. It is sufficient to say, perhaps as to both of those that neither statement has any bearing on any issue that you are trying." Held, that the impropriety of the argument of the plaintiff's counsel, to which the defendant expected, was not merely that the statements of the counsel were wrong (which they were) but that the use of them was an appeal to the jury to act in violation of their duty as jurors; that the instruction of the judge was not an instruction, (as it should have been) to disregard this improper argument; that the judge's charge did not cure the error; that the defendant's excep tion must be sustained; and that the defendant's counsel by taking an exception to the improper portion of the argument and asking the judge to instruct the jury to disregard it, had saved the defendant's right to have its exception sustained unless the judge cured the error which he did not do.

301 issue without a ruling is not the same as a ruling.821 Such conduct, particularly when no exception is then taken, does not create questions for the Supreme Judicial Court.822 Errors in the admission or exclusion of evidence or in rulings in trials generally, made subject to objections and exceptions, are frequently corrected by a later instruction.323 Such correction may or may not dispose of the strength of the exception.824 

Statements in argument concurring with the belief of the speaker in certain facts,325 or misquoting testimony 328 thus may be counteracted. The method of correcting such erroneous matters lies largely within the court's discretion; but correction is a right and duty;327 to such correction even if made without request, an attorney cannot object.328 If error is fully corrected by the trial judge, the party against whom the error existed, cannot complain that the error was not corrected by the specific words which that party has suggested.329 Hence if the opponent in his argument misquotes the evidence, and the judge in his charge corrects the error and instructs the jury to disregard the erroneous argument, the objector is not entitled to specific instructions as to the specific misquoted part of the evidence.880

A request for rulings need not be given in its exact phraseology; if the court covers the matter in his charge, the attorney making the request has no valid objection or exception.881
